projectOutComesReport:
This initiative focused on discovering what flow features govern the thrust and efficiency of fish fins, particularly high-frequency fins (flapping at 5+ Hz) with asymmetric motions. The discoveries support a better understanding of fish biology and ecology, enabling more responsible stewardship of rivers and oceans, and they also support the development of next-generation bio-inspired underwater vehicles. The three most significant findings of this initiative were 1) the optimal stiffness of a fish fin is speed-dependent, and for tuna-like tails, stiffness should increase with swimming speed squared, 2) the vortex wake behind high-frequency tails is unstable at certain frequency-amplitude combinations, leading to unavoidable side forces, and 3) swimming near a ground plane, such as a seabed, leads to side forces that are mitigated by tapered, undulatory fins. These findings offer hydrodynamic explanations for 1) why fish and fish-like robots need mechanisms to tune their own stiffness, 2) why fish and fish-like robots should use frequency, rather than amplitude, to adjust swimming speed, and 3) why near-ground (benthic) fish may have different shapes and swimming strategies than open water (pelagic) fish. The initiative also involved online and in-person interactive demos for 400+ middle and high school students. In the demos, students twisted a fish-like propulsor to explore the effects of tail stiffness. Finally, the initiative provided a launch point for the career of the PI. With data generated from this initiative, the PI secured funding to build one of the largest academic recirculating water channels in the world, which is currently under construction at the University of Virginia.

abstractText:
Internet of things (IoT) produces a large influx of streaming data. The high cost and long latency in shipping raw IoT data necessitates edge processing. The objective of this project is to safeguard IoT data during edge processing. It seeks to establish a trusted data path on the edge. As the data flows through the path, the proposed edge system ensures 1) data confidentiality: IoT data is only accessible to trusted parties; 2) integrity: all the data having arrived at the edge is exactly manipulated according to the planned processing; 3) verifiability: data flows and computations on the edge are verifiable to a trusted cloud backend. 

The project's research thrusts will be tightly integrated with its education and outreach plan, educating students on trustworthy computing scenarios as well as stimulating the public's interests in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM). There are plans to contribute fresh contents to curriculum; enhance student maker activities with in-situ IoT analytics; provide a summer course on IoT/Edge for local children; and, present relevant outreach at community IoT events. As IoT is revolutionizing modern society, the project aims toward more secure and efficient intelligence driven by IoT data.

projectOutComesReport:
This project targets new system software that safeguards edge systems, ensuring they process data efficiently, verifiably, and practically. Meanwhile, it integrates related educational activities into the research.

Through software and hardware research, the investigators have secured three key components at the edge: IO, storage, and compute. They have explored how to enable app code in Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), such as Arm TrustZone, to safely access OS services and accelerators. In response to recent breakthroughs in generative AI, they have investigated the efficient execution of language models, speech models, and diffusion on the edge.

Project Outcomes: The project has produced the following new software concepts and designs:

  1. Novel designs of deception-based defense to stop information leaks when TEE software uses external OS services.
  2. Novel designs for hardening the trusted computing base for accelerators at the edge.
  3. New methods for synthesizing replay-based device drivers in TEE.
  4. Novel designs for executing language models on resource-constrained edge devices.
  5. Novel designs for executing deep speech understanding on edge devices.

The project has resulted in numerous publications and multiple open-source codebases, including GPUReplay, Driverlet, and SpeechCache.

Broader Impacts: The PI has recruited multiple research assistants through this project, thereby training the future workforce with security-oriented and efficiency-oriented programming expertise. The PI has engaged undergraduate RAs, many of whom are underrepresented minorities, through this project. The PI has incorporated the experience and software outcomes into both graduate-level and undergraduate-level OS curricula at the University of Virginia. The technologies developed are likely to impact how the industry constructs and analyzes edge software. The research conducted is also likely to raise public awareness of security concerns in client and edge deployments.

abstractText:
Modern personalized information systems are black boxes to their users: computerized oracles give advice, but cannot be questioned. The lack of explanations for the personalized results has precluded broader adoption of personalization techniques in many important but high-risk domains, e.g., healthcare, education, and finance. This project aims to build a generic computational framework for explainable personalization, such that users will be aware of what information has been collected for customizing the system's output, and system developers can detect what type of personalized results will disclose users' privacy, e.g., unveiling his/her gender, age, or health status. This benefits both systems and users in the development of future information systems.

The proposed research focuses on two alternative perspectives, i.e., system-oriented and user-oriented explanation generation, in an adaptive fashion. The learning of personalization will be embedded with respect to the learning of explanation, so as to attain both personalization quality and explanation fidelity. In addition to building prototype systems to conduct user studies for evaluation, this project also takes a unique angle from econometric studies to assess the utility of the explanations via the users' revealed preferences. The value of explanation will be measured by the difference between the utilities of a user's decisions with and without explanations, which in turn enables adaptive evaluation and optimization of both explanation and personalization. The research activities will be incorporated into teaching materials in the area of information retrieval and machine learning. The planed outreach to high school students for education about online privacy would increase their awareness of potential risk of privacy breaches resulted from personalized systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Project Context and Goals

Modern recommendation systems often operate as "black boxes," providing suggestions without explaining the underlying reasoning or considering how users learn over time. This project aimed to bridge the gap between technical algorithm design and human economic behavior by transforming these systems into transparent, fair, and interactive partners for human decision-making. By integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with econometric theories of revealed preference, the research sought to create systems that are not only accurate but also trustworthy, equitable, and capable of natural conversation. The primary objective was to move beyond static models and account for the learning framework that occurs when both the AI and the human user refine their preferences through interaction.

Key Research Outcomes

The project achieved significant milestones in making AI explanations more useful and technically robust. We pioneered the concept of comparative explanations, which move beyond describing items in isolation to explaining why one item is ranked higher than another. In user studies, many participants found these comparative explanations helpful for decision-making than standard methods. To handle the complexity of modern AI, the team developed the Noise-Robust Active Ellipsoid Search (RAES) algorithm, which allows systems to learn effectively even when user feedback is non-stationary or inconsistent. Furthermore, as Large Language Models became central to the field, we developed modules to enhance their temporal awareness, ensuring recommendations account for the chronological order of user interactions. We also established statistical tools to measure the reliability of LLM outputs, ensuring consistent advice even when users phrase their queries differently.

Addressing Fairness and Ethics

A major pillar of this research was ensuring that personalization does not reinforce social stereotypes or create systemic disparities. We developed algorithms to decouple linguistic quality from protected attributes, such as gender or race, preventing the AI from generating lower-quality or biased explanations for specific demographic groups. In the final stages of the project, our research revealed that standard bias metrics often fail to predict "allocational harms" — real-world disparities in critical tasks like automated hiring or academic grading. To counter this, we developed decision-aware frameworks to audit these systems more accurately. Additionally, we explored the economic impact of recommendation policies on content creators, proving that relevance-driven systems can maintain user welfare even in highly competitive environments.

Broader Impacts and Training

The project significantly contributed to the STEM pipeline and the public scientific community. Over the course of the grant, the research provided training and support for over six PhD students, several Master’s students, and undergraduate researchers. These students gained leadership experience by mentoring peers and leading successful submissions to top-tier conferences such as ACL, NAACL, ICML, and NeurIPS. To ensure the benefits of the work reached the broader community, the team released open-source codebases for representation steering and bias evaluation on GitHub and shared findings through open-access pre-prints on ArXiv. Furthermore, the PIs integrated these latest research achievements into undergraduate courses on Information Retrieval, Reinforcement Learning, and Natural Language Processing, directly impacting the education of future computer scientists and economists.

abstractText:
Graphs are ubiquitous in myriad high-impact domains, e.g., social media platforms, collaboration networks, biological networks, and critical infrastructure systems. Recent years have witnessed a surge of research interests in developing deep learning algorithms (in particular graph convolution networks - GCNs) for graph data. By stacking multiple layers of neural network primitives, GCNs learn high-level feature representations and address graph-related applications in an end-to-end manner, achieving superior performance in various learning tasks. In particular, the graph convolution and graph pooling operations are considered as fundamental building blocks of GCNs. However, a vast majority of existing graph convolution and graph pooling operations are simple extensions of the corresponding operations from convolution neural networks. Therefore, they are insufficient to tackle the fundamental challenges brought by real-world graphs and advance high-impact graph mining applications. The primary goal of this project is to develop novel operations to improve the essential building blocks of deep learning algorithms for graphs, propelling the state-of-the-art graph mining and deep learning research to a new frontier and advancing graph-related applications from different disciplines.

This project proposes a class of novel graph convolution and pooling operations that can faithfully characterize the properties of real-world graphs from different perspectives, and build more tailored and powerful deep architectures in handling high-impact graph applications from different domains. First, it develops a family of trainable graph convolution operations that can integrate properties of real-world graphs from different aspects at the feature-level, edge-level, and node-level. Second, it investigates the problem of graph pooling to support graph-level analytical tasks and develops novel topology-aware graph pooling operations based on node sampling and node clustering. Third, it assesses the impact of proposed graph convolution and graph pooling operations by building more powerful and customized deep learning architectures for various common graph applications, such as graph anomaly detection and graph alignment. This project will be tightly integrated with newly developed undergraduate and graduate courses. The results and findings of this project will be disseminated through public datasets, open-source software repositories, journal and conference publications, special-purpose workshops or tutorials, as well as education and outreach activities.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern data often come in the form of networks or graphs, such as social networks, biological interaction networks, recommendation systems, and knowledge graphs. While deep learning has shown remarkable success for images and text, understanding and improving deep learning methods for graph-structured data remains challenging. This project addressed this challenge by studying how graph neural networks (GNNs) work at a fundamental level and by developing new methods that make them more reliable, interpretable, and broadly applicable.

Intellectual Merit.
Over the lifetime of this award, the project made significant contributions to the foundations of graph neural networks. We studied the basic operations that allow GNNs to learn from graph structure and identified fundamental limitations in existing approaches, such as loss of information as models become deeper. To overcome these issues, we developed new trainable graph operations that adapt to different graph structures and learning tasks. These advances improved the expressive power and stability of GNNs and clarified how graph topology and connectivity influence learning outcomes.

Beyond core model design, the project investigated how GNNs behave in realistic and challenging settings. We developed principled methods for learning from limited labeled data, enabling GNNs to perform well even when manual data annotation is scarce. We also studied robustness and generalization, addressing situations where models trained on one dataset must operate on different or evolving data distributions. In addition, we examined fairness, privacy, and interpretability in graph learning, proposing methods to understand and reduce bias, protect sensitive information, and explain model predictions.

These theoretical and methodological advances were accompanied by extensive empirical evaluation and benchmarking, helping the research community better understand when and why graph neural networks succeed or fail.

Broader Impacts.
The outcomes of this project extend well beyond theory. The developed techniques have been applied to a wide range of important real-world problems, including healthcare analytics, recommender systems, knowledge graph reasoning, anomaly detection, and scientific discovery. By improving robustness, fairness, and privacy, the project contributes to the responsible deployment of machine learning systems in high-stakes decision-making scenarios.

The project also had strong educational and workforce impacts. It supported and trained multiple graduate students, many of whom have gone on to academic and research careers, including tenure-track faculty positions. Research outcomes were integrated into undergraduate and graduate courses at the University of Virginia, directly benefiting students by exposing them to cutting-edge advances in graph machine learning. Several open-source tools and libraries produced by the project further lowered barriers for researchers and practitioners to adopt responsible graph learning methods.

Dissemination and Lasting Impact.
Across five years, this award supported a large body of peer-reviewed publications in leading venues in artificial intelligence, data mining, and machine learning. The results have been widely disseminated through conference presentations, tutorials, and surveys, shaping ongoing research directions in graph learning. Collectively, the project helped demystify how deep learning operates on graphs and laid a foundation for building more trustworthy, interpretable, and effective graph-based AI systems.

abstractText:
This Virtual Organization (VO) will facilitate communication and collaboration among CISE scientists currently involved in pandemic research through the NSF RAPID program. With the guidance of a Steering Committee composed of members from industry, academia, and government agencies, the VO will encourage the sharing of research results in a way not available without a concerted effort. The depth and breadth of multi-disciplinary collaboration enabled by this VO will be extended to include researchers, educators, and students interested in general topics related to pandemic planning and resilience. Utilizing a variety of dissemination platforms, the VO will harness the synergies of the CISE RAPID research programs to facilitate scientific advances and advance public health in the US and around the world.

The VO will: (i) facilitate the collection of a comprehensive collection of data sets, software tools, and documentation that can be shared by the research community; (ii) identification of new research efforts resulting from the cross fertilization of ideas from various subdisciplines of CISE research; (iii) a research roadmap that proposes research directions in CISE sciences that can lead to effective methods to prepare for and recover from future pandemics; and (iv) training and other pedagogic materials needed for educating future generations of scientists in topics related to pandemic preparedness, recovery, and resilience. The increased levels of collaboration fostered by this VO have the potential to result in innovative computational methods and technologies for dealing with future pandemics. The research roadmap will include identification of key research topics, risks, and gaps in the current R&D landscape that will significantly benefit the research community and serve as the blueprint for researchers, funding agencies, and policy makers on the role of information and communication technologies (ICT) in developing break-through solutions for pandemic resilience. While it is not possible to prevent pandemics completely, developing resilience techniques will enable society to prepare for and cope with the aftermath in a more effective manner.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
NSF PREPARE: Building a Resilient Future Through Pandemic Research

The NSF PREPARE (Pandemic Research for Resilience and Preparedness) project is a virtual organization dedicated to fostering a global community of researchers focused on pandemic preparedness. By promoting interdisciplinary collaboration and leveraging advanced computational tools, PREPARE aims to develop innovative solutions to enhance our ability to respond to and recover from pandemics.

Community Building: One of the primary achievements of NSF PREPARE is the creation of a robust, interdisciplinary community. The project has engaged scientists from various fields, including sociology, criminal justice, public health, and computational epidemiology. Domestic and global partnerships have been instrumental in broadening the scope of pandemic research and fostering international cooperation.

Workshops and Events: PREPARE has hosted numerous virtual workshops and events, attracting over 2000 participants. These workshops have covered a wide range of topics, from data access and computational resources to social, behavioral, economic, and governance issues during pandemics. The project has also organized specialized workshops on scalable computing and vaccine-preventable diseases, providing a platform for researchers to share their findings and collaborate on new initiatives.

Research and Publications: PREPARE has been active in promoting pandemic preparedness through various channels, including podcasts, YouTube, and its website. The "Science before the Storm" podcast has featured interviews with experts from diverse disciplines, fostering cross-disciplinary dialogue and collaboration. The project has also published research findings in reputable journals, such as the SPRINT team's paper in the journal Scientific Data.

Data Collection and Analysis: One component of PREPARE's work has been the collection and analysis of non-pharmaceutical intervention (NPI) data. Undergraduate students from the University of Virginia (UVA) have gathered county-level data on interventions like mask mandates, business closures, and school closures. This data is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of various measures and informing future pandemic responses.

Digital Twins of Epidemic outbreaks: PREPARE has contributed to the development of synthetic datasets (digital twins) that simulate realistic disease outbreaks, based on feedback from the community as part of the roadmap development. This is useful for development of new epidemiological and machine learning tools. This will also allow researchers to develop and test privacy-preserving methods for predicting infection risks. One such dataset was used to support development of new privacy-enhancing technologies, as part of  the US-UK Prize Challenge. This initiative highlights the importance of balancing data privacy with the need for accurate and timely public health information.

Impact and Future Directions: The impact of NSF PREPARE extends beyond immediate research outcomes. By building a global network of researchers and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration, the project is laying the groundwork for a more resilient and prepared society. The Research Roadmap developed by PREPARE outlines key research topics, risks, and gaps in the current landscape, serving as a blueprint for future efforts in pandemic resilience.

In summary, NSF PREPARE is making significant contributions to pandemic preparedness by fostering a collaborative research community, advancing educational initiatives, and developing innovative solutions to public health challenges. Through its ongoing efforts, PREPARE is helping to ensure that we are better equipped to face future pandemics with resilience and preparedness.

abstractText:
With the advances in data collection techniques, large amounts of multimodal data collected from multiple sources are widely available, including text, images, video, and audio. Such multimodal data can provide complementary information that can reveal the fundamental characteristics of applications. Thus, multimodal machine learning which builds models that can process and relate information from multiple modalities has become an active research area. Extensive works have been developed to combine different modalities, learn joint representations to exploit complementarity and redundancy of multiple modalities, and fuse information to perform prediction tasks. However, effectively integrating and analyzing multimodal data remains a challenging problem, especially when the data is incomplete. Missing modality is a common issue in real-world multimodal data, which can be caused by various reasons such as sensor damage, data corruption, and human mistakes in recording. Such incomplete data imposes significant challenges to multimodal machine learning. This project develops a multimodal machine learning framework that formulates a new fundamental structure to facilitate the complex information extraction and integration from multimodal data with incomplete modalities for classification and prediction. This project has significant potential to advance the theory and practice of multimodal machine learning, with strong implication in targeted domains such as Information Systems, Engineering, and Biomedicine. 


Technically, this project develops a framework that exploits the powerful representational features of graph based structure to model the complex interaction between heterogeneous datasets, promoting deep information fusion and sustainable data analysis. The proposed multimodal machine learning approach formulates a new fundamental framework that enables the complex information extraction and integration from multimodal data with incomplete modalities.  A multi-level hypergraph structure is designed to model the multimodal data with incompleteness, and a multistage data fusion framework is developed to enable a transductive learning process through which all heterogeneous data points with different missing data conditions are projected into the same embedding space and multi-modalities are fused along the way. The proposed method models the complex intra and inter modality relationships, extract complementary multimodal information, and fuse the information from multiple subspaces to a unified representation. The proposed research develops a unique strategy for learning on data with incomplete modalities, without data deletion or data imputation. The proposed research enables the information from incomplete modalities to be effectively included in the learning process when one or more modalities are missing. Moreover, the proposed interpretation method utilizes the rich semantics learned from the data to interpret the model behaviors behind a particular prediction decision. This increases the transparency of the proposed approach and also contributes towards explainable machine learning.

abstractText:
The promise of machine learning is that it will improve the operation of systems across a variety of domains, such as agriculture, transportation, and medicine.  With that promise comes the risk that such systems will not operate as intended, which may lead to harm to individuals or society.  The project's impacts are in mitigating these risks by developing practical methods for assuring the correct operation of machine-learning systems.  While risk is not unique to systems that incorporate machine learning, such systems present additional challenges to assuring their correct operation.   Consider a camera-based driving system that aims to recognize a stop sign.  Such a system must correctly identify a sign from among the enormous number of possible images while considering variables, such as, angle, lighting, distance, and any obstructions.  Assuring such a system is correct requires evaluating the system on all such images, but it would take many years to evaluate each in turn on even the fastest computer.  The project's novelties are in assuring correct behavior for groups of inputs collectively, which promises to make the assurance process practical.

This project develops techniques to accelerate verification algorithms for assuring the correct operation of machine-learning models.  First, these techniques exploit the fact that the system will only ever be required to consider a small fraction of the set of all possible inputs.  Those inputs can be described symbolically and considered in groups to accelerate verification.  Second, these techniques exploit the fact that a system may respond to different inputs by performing identical processing.   Focusing verification on the processing performed by the system, rather than the inputs that are processed, allows verification to group sets of inputs to further accelerate assurance. The project develops a series of prototype implementations and benchmarks that demonstrate the utility and cost-effectiveness of the research, and that can be leveraged by the broader community for comparative evaluation.

projectOutComesReport:
Neural networks are improving rapidly in their ability to accurately approximate complex functions and can exceed the performance of human-built solutions in a number of domains.  To gain the benefits of increased performance, developers across a variety of sectors including: transportation, medicine, defense, and financial, are considering deploying neural networks as components of their systems.  To do so confidently requires evidence that the networks work as intended.  Recent research has adapted formal verification techniques to target the rigorous analysis of neural networks for this purpose, but these techniques perform highly over-approximative reasoning about about network behavior which leads to either a failure to confirm desired behavior or false reports of erroneous behavior, thereby limiting the usefulness of the techniques.  To address this challenge, we pursued two complementary prongs of research.

First, we exploit emerging techniques for training latent-space generative models for a dataset and compose those models with networks trained to make predictions from that dataset.  Verifying such a composition leads to a significant reduction in over-approximation, which in turn leads directly to a reduction in false error reports and to increases in the verification problems that can be solved.  This class of distribution-aware verification and validation techniques has broad applicability, for instance, to black box test adequacy metrics and principled test generation techniques for neural networks.

Second, reducing over-approximation means that the verifier need not reason about behavior that is infeasible relative to the generative model.  This allows for the development of cost-effective optimization techniques that seek to constrain the space of neural activations over which the verification algorithm operates.  We have developed a suite of techniques that perform such optimization, by identifying and increasing the number of stable neurons, at network training time and also on-the-fly during verification.  These methods have been integrated into state-of-the-art neural network verifiers.

This project has introduced a completely new family of methods for verification and validation of neural networks.  The results and findings establish a solid theoretical foundation for future work, develop engineering solutions that significantly advance the state-of-the-art, and that freely available in open-source implementations that researchers and practitioners can use them and to promote open-science.

More broadly the project has advanced science and engineering in support of more trustworthy machine learning which is an important area of need for the nation.

abstractText:
The long-term vision of this project is to create a multi-campus data collection and sharing infrastructure for use by machine-learning cybersecurity and privacy researchers. These datasets will be multimodal in nature (network logs, host logs, authentication logs for kill-chain detection), provide continuous data (for long-term temporal and topological analysis), and be timely in nature (necessary to handle the constantly evolving nature of cyber-attacks). The specific initial steps under this Planning Grant are: (i) organize a workshop to engage the community to formulate a vision and roadmap for this infrastructure and to discuss legal, ethical, privacy, organizational and sustainability considerations, and (ii) create a team of multiple data providers and data users and submit a Grand Ensemble CCRI proposal to build and use the data infrastructure.

The envisioned infrastructure will be invaluable for detecting zero-day (new, previously unseen) attacks and large-scale attacks with complex kill-chains, e.g., the Wannacry ransomware attack, Mirai Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks and Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) attacks. It will be built with input from a selected group of early adopters, i.e., data users who can develop and test their machine learning techniques. Later, the Shibboleth Single Sign-On Access of Incommon Federation members will be used to broaden access to the entire CISE community. Community outreach and dissemination activities are part of the planning grant workshop. A number of undergraduate and graduate students will participate in this project at University of Virginia (UVA), Indiana University (IU), and George Washington University (GWU). Diversity enhancing activities are planned through centers at UVA and IU, and the GWU co-PI’s research Lab.

projectOutComesReport:
The goals of the project, "CCRI: Planning: Towards Building a Community Data Infrastructure for Cybersecurity Research," was the development of a plan to create a multi-campus and sharing research infrastructure for use by machine-learning cybersecurity and privacy researchers, and the formulation of a vision and roadmap for this infrastructure and to discuss legal, ethical, privacy, organizational and sustainability considerations. Originally planned as a one-year exercise, NSF granted a one-year, no-cost extension because of COVID.

The project had several outcomes. The first was the organization of a workshop that brought together academic researchers, government funding agencies, and industry to formulate a vision and roadmap for creating a multi-campus data collection and sharing infrastructure for use by machine-learning cybersecurity and privacy researchers. The virtual workshop was held on July 27?28, 2021. There were 83 workshop participants.The result of the workshop was a report that discussed key questions and concerns that should be addressed in designing and building the infrastructure. Key questions were:

  • What data to collect?
  • The importance of preserving the privacy of individuals who contribute data.
  • The tension between making the data open, preserving privacy, and supporting the reproducibility of research results, and
  • How to sustain the collection, curation, and storage of these enormous data sets.

The second project outcome was the organization of a workshop, ML for Cybersecurity (ML4Cyber), held in conjunction with the 2022 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) located in Baltimore, Maryland. The workshop's goal was to build a mutual comprehensive awareness of the problem and solution spaces across the greater ML community and the Cybersecurity/ML for Cybersecurity communities. There were five contributed papers, two keynote presentations, nine short presentations, and nine posters. The workshop included a panel discussion on benchmark datasets,

The third outcome was the June 2022 grant proposal submission to the CISE Community Research Infrastructure Program (CCRI). The proposal targeted the Grand Community Infrastructure (Grand) class of awards. The collaborative proposal was a joint effort of the University of Virginia, Virginia Tech, and Old Dominion University. While NSF declined to fund the proposal, the PIs are revising the proposal to address some of the feedback received from the reviewers. This revision will be submitted to the new Community Infrastructure in Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CIRC) program.

This award provides partial support to help defray the expenses of participants in the 2020 East Coast Operator Algebra Symposium (ECOAS), which will be held on the University of Virginia campus in Charlottesville, Virginia, October 17-18, 2020. The symposium expects to host between 40-60 participants, including many graduate students and postdocs. This will be the eighteenth annual meeting in the East Coast Operator Algebra Symposium series. 

The conference focuses on operator algebras (C* and von Neumann algebras) and non-commutative geometry. This year we are particularly focusing on connections to quantum information theory, quantum algebra, conformal field theory, unitary representation theory, deformation/rigidity theory, and C*-classification. The ECOAS enables participants to become acquainted with the modern developments in operator algebras, non-commutative geometry, and neighboring disciplines.  A major goal is to highlight the work of early-career researchers and facilitate them networking with other junior as well as senior researchers. More information can be found at the conference website: https://sites.google.com/view/ecoas2020uva/home?authuser=2.

projectOutComesReport:
The purpose of this grant was to defray costs for a series of confernces "East Coast Operator Algebras Symposium" hosted at Michigan State University in 2023 and Purdue University in 2024.

 

The intellectual merit of these conferences is encapsulated by the series of talks- here researchers in the field present their current results in operator algebras and adjacent fields. Operator algebras is subdiscipline of mathematics that forms the basis for quantum mechanics. It also has applications to statistical mechanics and knot theory. Talks at conferences like these are one of the primary ways in which researchers in the field present their results to the public and it one of the major avenues in which researchers in the field gain exposure to the significant and important results in the subject.

 

This particular series of conferences is aimed at early-career researchers, especially graduate students. The funds from this grant were primarily aimed at reimbursing their travel and lodging. Participation and attendance in conferences like these are vital to the long-term success of early-career researchers (especially graduate students), as it provides them not only the exposure to important topics alluded to above, but also gives them an opportunity to form career connections which frequently turn into collaboration or mentorship. These conferences form the basis for training that ultimately turns newcomers in the field into the next generation of experts.

abstractText:
Knowledge repository refers to a machine-readable structure that stores knowledge about various entities (e.g., organizations, events, genes), which facilitates efficient information seeking.  In many domains, knowledge varies with respect to contexts, and a flat structure that is commonly adopted by existing knowledge repositories cannot capture the complicated knowledge associated with different contexts.  To make knowledge resources more findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR), this project plans to conceptualize a new structure, Knowledge Hypercube, for organizing and retrieving knowledge that could support complex applications in various domains.  A knowledge hybercube organizes knowledge with respect to selected important dimensions (e.g., time, locations, conditions), and thus it allows people to easily access knowledge in any context, encapsulate distinctive entities and facts, and conduct cross-dimensional comparison and inference.  This project impacts how people find and use knowledge, advances knowledge-based data analytics approaches, and benefits a wide range of domains which have gigantic literature and unsolved complex tasks by building a bridge between them. Knowledge hypercubes can also support educational innovation and contributes to educational tasks such as knowledge tracing.
 
The major objective of this proposal is to form a paradigm of mining knowledge hybercubes from massive collection of text documents and leveraging such hybercubes for complex exploration and prediction tasks. To meet this goal, this project tackles a series of technical challenges. First, to automatically construct a knowledge hypercube from massive texts, innovative weakly supervised approaches are designed to organize text documents based on the hypercube structure, extract open entity and relationship information and organize cell-specific and cross-cell knowledge in a multi-dimensional manner.  Second, novel refinement approaches are developed to automatically verify the information quality within and across cells in knowledge hypercubes by cross-checking within the hypercubes and with external information.  Third, knowledge hypercubes motivate the development towards new discovery and learning tasks. In particular, the project introduces an automatic knowledge search pipeline for leveraging knowledge hypercubes for downstream prediction tasks, and a hypothesis generation approach for scoring unknown associations between concepts.  The planned paradigm is realized in two specific domains (i.e., biomedical and news events), demonstrating the power of knowledge hypercubes to enable new insights into these domains.

abstractText:
This project develops a novel online learning based framework for distributed low-cost devices to efficiently and effectively access the shared spectrum without spectrum sensing. It specifically focuses on no-sensing devices that do not have the powerful radio-frequency (RF) components to enable wideband spectrum sensing, and addresses the cross-technology spectrum access problem in a decentralized setting. A pertinent application the proposed solution addresses is the dynamic spectrum access of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices that are deployed in either unlicensed or lightly licensed spectrum, in which the distributed IoT devices need to coexist with other active systems. The no-sensing spectrum access and sharing framework has the potential to revolutionize the operation and management of modern and future wireless networks, considerably enhance the spectrum utilization efficiency, and dramatically alleviate the constantly increasing pressure on the limited radio spectrum. The cross disciplinary nature of the research would naturally translate into case studies and projects in a number of undergraduate and graduate level courses taught by the PIs in areas of communications, machine learning, and networking.

This project aims to develop a suite of online learning based spectrum access algorithms for no-sensing devices to coexist with other active systems. The first study focuses on improving the learning efficiency by introducing the best arm identification framework and proposing meta-learning and good channel identification algorithms. The second thrust is devoted to designing spectrum access mechanisms that can seamlessly integrate hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ). Novel algorithms will be designed to learn the optimal sequence of channels for possible retransmissions, and enhanced for fine-grained control that captures the coding level behavior of HARQ. The last thread of investigation considers multi-user multi-technology coexistence and will develop implicit-communication based distributed spectrum access algorithms. Finally, a thorough validation of the algorithms and spectrum access schemes will be performed using a lab testbed and real-world datasets.

Summary

This project aimed to develop online learning-based frameworks for dynamic spectrum access in wireless networks, particularly for low-cost devices without sensing capabilities. By advancing reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms, the project addressed long-term radio resource management and coexistence challenges in shared spectrum environments. Over the project period, we developed novel average-reward RL methods, multi-agent decision transformers, and federated bandit frameworks, each designed to enhance learning efficiency and deployment feasibility in real-world wireless systems. The outcomes of this work have influenced both machine learning and wireless communications communities, advancing AI-native spectrum management while contributing to the interdisciplinary workforce of the future.

Intellectual Merit

The key intellectual contributions of the project include:

1. Development of Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Wireless Systems: We introduced an average-reward framework to replace traditional discounted RL in radio resource management. This addressed a fundamental mismatch between RL objectives and long-term wireless performance, resulting in improved alignment with quality-of-service requirements and demonstrated performance gains in RAN slicing applications.

2. Introduction of Multi-Agent Decision Transformers for Power Control: We developed a transformer-based, offline multi-agent RL method capable of decentralized control using only partial and delayed channel information. This approach achieved performance comparable to centralized optimization and demonstrated superior safety, stability, and convergence over online RL methods.

3. Advances in Federated and Offline Bandit Algorithms: We extended federated bandits and offline RL frameworks to spectrum access scenarios, enabling collaborative learning across clients without raw data sharing. These methods achieved near-optimal regret with minimal communication and opened pathways for real-world deployment in cognitive radio networks.

Broader Impacts

The broader impacts of the project include technological, educational, and societal contributions:

1. Technological Impact: The algorithms developed in this project are compatible with emerging 6G architectures and spectrum-sharing platforms, supporting the transition toward AI-driven wireless infrastructure. The integration of offline RL and decision transformers provides new tools for safe, deployable network control.

2. Workforce Development: The project trained multiple Ph.D. students in both machine learning and wireless communications, fostering interdisciplinary expertise that is rare in current research ecosystems. Students gained skills in RL theory, wireless simulation, and algorithm implementation, preparing them for leadership roles in academia and industry.

3. Cross-Disciplinary Influence: The frameworks developed here extend beyond wireless engineering to domains such as autonomous systems, smart grids, logistics, and distributed robotics. By emphasizing long-term optimization and safe offline learning, the project contributed to broader AI research focused on reliability and decentralized decision-making.

Conclusion

In summary, this project successfully advanced the integration of reinforcement learning and spectrum engineering, producing new theoretical frameworks and practical algorithms for dynamic spectrum access. The intellectual outcomes reshaped how long-term wireless spectrum optimization is approached, while broader impacts extended into workforce development and cross-disciplinary AI applications. The findings are poised to influence future AI-native wireless standards and enable safer, data-driven control in cyber-physical systems. This project has laid a foundation for continued innovation at the intersection of machine learning, communications, and real-world deployment.

abstractText:
STEM ethics education is an integral element of the effort to facilitate ethical science and protect against research misconduct. The Online Ethics Center is the nation's premier online platform for storing, curating, and discussing state-of-the-art information about teaching research ethics, Responsible Conduct of Research, and fostering ethical cultures within science and engineering. The goal of this project is to update and improve the Online Ethics Center (OEC). The investigators will do so by better engaging faculty and administrators who are new to teaching ethics, and by conducting a series of workshops with the user community that will enable them to gather multiple types of social science data and systematically assess how the OEC can better meet the needs of its constituents. Grant funds will also be used for regular site maintenance and to hire an expert external evaluator to formally assess OEC's activities and aid the investigators in improving site usability and updating the resource collection that they provide. Together, these efforts will help improve the quality of STEM ethics education and encourage and equip U.S. researchers to engage in ethical scientific practice.

The main goal of this project is to update and improve the Online Ethics Center (OEC). To do so, the investigators will engage in a systematic social scientific assessment of the OEC and its user community. This will enable them to understand how the site can be modified to better meet the needs of its constituents and to provide more and higher quality resources to its user community. They will do so first by gathering data at the STEM ethics education workshops that they will organize, and through interviewing and surveying members of their user communities. Second, the investigators would solicit, develop, and curate new and enhanced resources for advancing STEM ethics education. Third, the investigators will fund ongoing site maintenance while significantly improving its functionality. Finally, the investigators will hire a part-time consultant to act as an expert evaluator to formally assess: (1) site usability; (2) user demographics; (3) visitors' purposes for coming to the site and whether they were able to find what they were looking for; (4) the uses to which visitors put site resources; (5) which aspects of the OEC users find most and least helpful; and (6) how the resource collection might be improved.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The Online Ethics Center (OEC) provides quality Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) ethics education resources and connects practitioners, researchers, and educators to promote learning and advance understanding of responsible research and ethical practice in STEM. 

Awarded in 2018 to the National Academy of Engineering, the project called “Transforming Ethics Education: Connecting STEM Faculty, Research Administrators and Ethics Resources through the Online Ethics Center sought to: “(1) help transform education in the responsible conduct of research (RCR), (2) advance the CCE STEM program mission of fostering an ethical culture in education and practice, and (3) become a key, self-sustaining part of a comprehensive approach to improve the ethical culture and integrity at US research and STEM education institutions.” 

These goals were formulated to serve two audiences: science and engineering (S&E) faculty new to teaching ethics, and university administrators responsible for implementing RCR requirements. With these goals in mind, the OEC leadership developed two objectives for the project: “(1) engage and equip S&E faculty with tools and resources that will enable them to infuse ethical values and training in their disciplinary courses, and (2) engage and support the work of university administrators and others responsible for educating students, postdocs, and faculty about research integrity and RCR and for facilitating a culture of ethical and responsible research and practice at their institutions.” 

In 2021, the decision was made to transition the OEC from the NAE to the University of Virginia (UVA). This included not only changing its institutional home, but also moving its technology infrastructure, the content management system. 

The OEC Advisory Group (AG) has long been an important input and asset to the OEC. Two notable additions to the AG were John Unsworth, Dean of Libraries and University Librarian; and Phillip Bourne, Dean, School of Data Science & Professor of Biomedical Engineering. Having senior UVA administrators on the AG helped to solidify the new institutional arrangement with UVA. Arizona State University (ASU) and Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) remained substantial inputs, with ASU’s Karin Ellison and IIT’s Kelly Laas serving as Co-Principal Investigators. They supported the development of webinars, forums, and other interactive components of the OEC; focused on sustainability by leading the disposition of OEC resources into the UVA open digital repository called LibraOpen; developed bibliographies, teaching materials, and other resources for the OEC; and managed the Ethics Education Library. 

The OEC Editorial Board (EB) worked to identify and review additional materials for the OEC repository, and helped develop and test enhancements to the site to better reach intended audiences and communities. The EB ecompasses eigh areas: Engineering; Life and Environmental Science; computer, Mathematics, and Physical Sciences; Social and Behavioral Sciences; Research Ethics; International Perspectives; Social Justice; and Outreach and Engagement. 

OEC's webinar series: “Working Ethics into the Conversation”, brings together students, academics, and professionals in conversations about ethics. The first webinar, “What Is Professional Responsibility in Engineering?”, was led by OEC AG member Dr. Michael Loui, Professor Emeritus of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, joined by discussant Dr. Jeff Brown, Associate Professor of Civil Engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Over 80 persons registered for the webinar, with 65 attending. This webinar laid a solid foundation for subsequent webinars, hosted by Azita Hirsa, Senior Lecturer, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. The webinar series  has become a major factor for OEC impact (along with the Communities of Practice). 

One of the most exciting aspects of this OEC project has been the development and growth of the Communities of Practice (COPs). To stimulate the development of the COPs, the OEC created the OEC Fellows. These OEC Fellows, currently at nine, are assembling groups of OEC members who share specific interests related to research, teaching, and managing STEM related research embedded in an ethics framework. Seven COPs were developed in the following order (along with the lead OEC Fellow(s): (1) Biomedical Engineering Ethics (Dr. Andrew O. Brightman, Purdue University, Weldon School of Biomedical Engineering); (2) Scholars, Educators, and Administrators Fostering Research Integrity (Dr. Julie Simpson, University of New Hampshire); (3) Teaching Ethics to Engineering Students (Dr. Laura Grossenbacher (University of Wisconsin-Madison, College of Engineering) and Dr. Rider Foley (University of Virginia, Department of Engineering and Society); (4) Data Epistemologies and Interpretive Ethics (Dr. Natasha Mauthner (Newcastle University) and Dr. Dena Plemmons (University of California, Riverside); (5) Developing and Implementing Institutional RECR Plans (Katie Bode-Lang, Penn State University); (6) Engineering & Social Justice (Elliot P. Douglas, Ph.D., F. ASEE, University of Florida and J. Britt Holbrook, New Jersey Institute of Technology); and (7) Data Ethics (Dr. Victoria Stodden, University of Southern California, Viterbi School of Engineering). 

The OEC is now functioning as a self-sustaining project of the University of Virginia’s School of Engineering, Department of Engineering and Society, and supported by the work of volunteers from across the United States.

abstractText:
Humans are intensely social beings who live in complex groups. One major challenge for the human brain is to enable us to effectively navigate and benefit from this complex social environment. This project will examine the early development of the brain systems that enable us to process and learn from third-person social interactions. The researchers will investigate brain, cognitive and behavioral development during infancy with a specific focus on observing social interactions. By revealing how brain processes underpinning early infant social and cognitive development unfold, this research will fill an important gap in our knowledge and has broad implications for understanding healthy and atypical development. The project is multidisciplinary in nature as it uses a cutting-edge approach combining neuroscience, behavioral and experience-sampling methods. The findings will be broadly applicable to multiple disciplines and will inform the brain, cognitive and social sciences. The planned experiments will provide valuable research opportunities and unique training for students. The project has implications for early education, intervention and may help guide public policy decisions concerning infant and child development.

The current project tests the hypothesis that brain systems in prefrontal and temporal cortex begin to specialize in third-person social interaction processing during infancy. To this end, this project will (i) examine developmental changes in the neural processing of social interactions during infancy using a multi-method neuroimaging approach, (ii) assess the characteristics and functions of this brain system, (iii) investigate variability and the role of experience in the emergence of this brain system in a longitudinal study. Uncovering the neurodevelopmental roots of social interaction processing in infancy will have a wide-ranging impact as it informs our understanding of human nature and cognition in profound ways and has the potential to inspire further research into social intelligence in man and machines. Through this project and its findings it will be possible to foster a better understanding among the public of how important early social development occurs and what role brain development and experience plays.

projectOutComesReport:
From our first days of life, we are immersed in a rich social world. Infants watch parents interact, observe emotional exchanges, and respond to smiles and laughter - all before they can speak a single word. But how does the infant brain make sense of this complex social landscape? This project set out to answer a fundamental question: How do we develop the ability to understand and navigate the social world around us?

Uncovering the Social Brain in Infancy

Using non-invasive brain imaging techniques, our research team examined how infants' brains process social information during the critical first years of life. What we discovered challenges previous assumptions and reveals that babies are far more sophisticated social learners than we once believed.

Our findings demonstrate that specific brain regions - particularly areas in the prefrontal cortex at the front of the brain - are remarkably active when infants observe social interactions. The medial prefrontal cortex, a region associated with thinking about oneself and others, emerges as a crucial hub for social processing even in infancy. We discovered that this brain region helps infants develop what we call the "social self" - an understanding that they are social beings embedded in relationships with others.

One of our most striking discoveries involved how infants respond to social smiles. When we measured brain activity in the dorso-medial prefrontal cortex as infants viewed smiling faces, we found that stronger responses predicted how sociable those children would become as they developed. In essence, we identified a neural signature in infancy that forecasts future social behavior - opening new possibilities for understanding individual differences in social development.

The Power of Positive Social Experiences

Perhaps most exciting was our discovery of how positive social experiences shape the developing brain. We found that social smiling and laughter don't just make babies happy - they literally strengthen the brain's social circuitry. Specifically, these joyful interactions enhance connectivity in what neuroscientists call the "default mode network," a system of brain regions that activates when we think about ourselves, remember the past, or imagine social scenarios. This finding reveals a profound truth: warm, positive social interactions during infancy are building the neural architecture that will support social thinking throughout life.

We also investigated how infants process third-party social interactions - situations where they observe two other people interacting with each other. This ability is fundamental to social learning and understanding complex social dynamics. Our research revealed that even young infants possess dedicated brain systems for making sense of these observed interactions, suggesting that humans are biologically prepared to learn from the social world around them.

From Biology to Behavior

Our research uncovered surprising connections between biology and social development. In collaboration with microbiome researchers, we discovered that the composition of gut bacteria in newborns is associated with both brain connectivity patterns and behavioral temperament. This finding suggests that the biological foundations of social behavior may be even more complex than previously imagined, involving not just brain development but also the microbial communities that inhabit our bodies.

Intellectual Merit: Advancing Scientific Knowledge

This project made significant contributions to developmental neuroscience and our understanding of human social cognition. We challenged long-held assumptions by demonstrating continuity between infant and adult social perception systems, rather than the dramatic developmental shifts previously theorized. By integrating findings across evolutionary biology, developmental psychology, and neuroscience, we developed a novel theoretical framework proposing that humans possess a "motivated social brain" - that our brains are not just capable of processing social information but are actively driven to seek it out through "social curiosity." This framework advances knowledge about what makes humans uniquely social and explains the neurodevelopmental origins of social interaction processing. Our work provides the first comprehensive account of how the social self emerges in the developing brain and establishes new directions for research on early social cognition.

Broader Impacts: Benefits to Society

This research has important implications beyond the laboratory. Our finding that maternal sensitivity shapes infants' neural responses to emotion underscores the profound importance of responsive, warm caregiving - information that can inform parenting education programs and early childhood policies. Understanding how positive social experiences strengthen brain connectivity provides evidence-based support for initiatives promoting nurturing early relationships.

The project trained multiple graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in advanced neuroscience methods, contributing to workforce development in STEM fields. We disseminated findings through 13 peer-reviewed publications in leading scientific journals, ensuring broad impact on the scientific community. By making our research accessible to the public, we help families and educators understand how early experiences shape the developing social brain, ultimately supporting efforts to nurture healthy social development in all children.

abstractText:
This research project is supported by the EHR Core Research (ECR) program, which supports work that advances fundamental research on STEM learning and learning environments, broadening participation in STEM, and STEM workforce development.

In the last decade, there has been a tremendous increase in the use of video for preparing teachers and studying teaching quality. Prominent approaches to summative evaluation of teaching candidates and beginning teachers feature video recordings of instructional practices. In addition, large-scale research studies have included video of instruction. Teacher preparation programs increasingly use video in methods courses and for formative assessment purposes. Moreover, the growing use of interactive simulation in pre-service preparation and in-service professional development relies on having video recorded examples of exemplary instructional practices. Despite the significant growth in the use of video to measure and promote instructional quality in recent years, there remain some key challenges to employing it at scale. First, it is very time-consuming for trained human raters to view hundreds of hours of video recorded lessons. Second, financial costs and time demands increase with the use of multiple human raters per video. Third, manually cataloging, labeling, and indexing large volumes of classroom video for later viewing is time consuming. Recent advances in computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning may provide solutions to these challenges and could make the process of analyzing and scoring videos more efficient. In particular, deep learning has become the state-of-the-art choice in problems related to analyzing the content of video. This proposed NSF Core Research study will draw on videos of elementary mathematics instruction that were collected for two NSF-funded studies that featured the Mathematics-Scan (M-Scan) classroom observation tool. The research will use these videos to explore several ways that deep neural networks can be used to classify instructional activities in videos of math instruction.

This study will advance knowledge and understanding by examining the degree to which three types of artificial neural networks can accurately classify (a) objects and (b) instructional activities in videos of elementary mathematics instruction. For example, it may be straightforward for neural networks to determine whether an elementary teacher is engaged in lecture vs. facilitating discussion with students. On the other hand, it may be harder for such networks to assess the ways teachers represent math content, the nature of their questions, and whether student gestures signify understanding. The research design concerns three aspects of using computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning: (a) the type of neural network, (b) the type of video label (i.e., object labels and instructional activity labels), and (c) the subject of math instruction (e.g., number and operations; patterns, functions, and algebra; geometry). A few types of neural networks have recently proven effective for video classification: convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks, and hybrid CNN-LSTMs. Ultimately, this project is aimed at beginning to build systematic infrastructure for classifying videos of classroom instruction at scale in efficient and affordable ways. The findings will potentially have key implications for (a) large-scale research studies that feature videos of instruction and (b) pre-service teacher preparation programs, in-service professional development activities, and efforts to evaluate teaching candidates and practicing teachers. In particular, the results from this study will inform decisions about the types of neural networks that can be used to correctly classify videos of instruction and the practical limitations of using networks for this purpose.

projectOutComesReport:
In a main set of analyses for this study, we reported results from training and testing two related neural network models. We used 80 hours of annotated videos of elementary mathematics and reading instruction to train the two network models and 20 hours of annotated videos to test these models. We compared the two models based on a standard measurement metric–the F1 score. We found that the Background Suppression Network model generated adequate levels of classification accuracy (F1 scores of 0.50 or higher) for several of our 24 instructional activity labels. The Improved Background Suppression Network Model for Classrooms generated improved levels of classification accuracy (0.50 to 0.70) for four main activity labels: whole group instruction, small group instruction, individual student work, and transitions (i.e., no instruction).

In a second set of analyses, we examined correlations between our neural network output (related to the 24 instructional activity labels) and human ratings of the same elementary mathematics lessons that were used to generate the neural network output and that were previously scored using the Mathematics-Scan (M-Scan) classroom observation instrument. We found significant agreement between neural network and human ratings for three M-Scan dimensions: cognitive demand, problem solving, and use of representations. This could potentially lead to a 33% reduction in human effort in scoring classroom observations using M-Scan when supplemented with automated machine scoring.

In a third set of analyses, we investigated which of our 24 focal instructional activities helped contribute to more accurate automated lesson ratings of ambitious mathematics instruction with M-Scan as compared to human-rated lessons. We reported that even fine-grained, low-inference instructional activities, such as the time students spend talking or standing during a lesson, may serve as a productive base for training these emerging technologies to predict features of mathematics instructional quality. 

In terms of intellectual merit, our study advanced knowledge and understanding by examining the degree to which different neural networks can accurately classify instructional activities in videos of elementary mathematics and reading instruction. Our study also considered whether classification accuracy was affected by the subject of mathematics instruction. We found an improvement in network model performance for one mathematical content domain: Data Analysis and Probability. Our study’s interdisciplinary approach integrated a mathematics education component and an artificial intelligence component. Few previous research studies have used such an approach to investigate the potential role of neural networks in classifying videos of instruction.

With regard to broader impacts, we analyzed whether neural network classification of teachers’ instructional activities varied based on teacher race and skin tone and whether differently-balanced training datasets influenced the performance of the neural network. We found that, under typical classroom lighting conditions, the network model performed equally well regardless of teacher race or skin tone. In addition, our results suggest that the balance of the training dataset with respect to teacher skin tone and race has a mixed, but negligible impact on the network model’s performance.

The results from this study will inform decisions about the types of network model that can be used to correctly classify videos of instruction and the practical limitations of using networks for this purpose. Further, while our project focuses on elementary mathematics videos, it has potential applications for videos of instruction in other content areas and at other schooling levels. 

In a fourth set of analyses, we trained a multimodal neural network model (i.e., a transformer model) with 40 hours of annotated video and audio data and tested the multimodal model with 10 hours of data. In preliminary analyses, we found that training a transformer model with video and audio data led to high levels of classification accuracy (F1 scores of 0.85 or higher for most video labels and F1 scores of 0.60 or higher for most audio labels).

We developed a teacher dashboard prototype that provides virtual coaching to elementary teachers on four dimensions of quality aligned with the Mathematical Quality of Instruction (MQI) classroom observation tool. The virtual coaching proceeds through multiple phases. Before the coaching cycle begins, a teacher uploads a video of an elementary mathematics lesson to the prototype. Then, the transformer model analyzes the video and automatically produces output based on the frequency of several audio- and video-based activity labels.

In the first phase of the coaching cycle, the teacher interacts with a virtual coach to choose one of the four dimensions aligned with the MQI to focus on throughout the cycle. In the second phase, the virtual coach shares a subset of four network outputs with the teacher through the prototype at the lesson level. In the third and final phase, the elementary teacher is prompted by the virtual coach to view the video of this particular lesson and analyze more closely each of the four metrics one at a time as they review the lesson video

abstractText:
Rapid warming in boreal forests has driven diverse ecosystem changes in recent decades, including permafrost thaw, longer non-frozen seasons, and warmer summers. The impact of these changes on the carbon balance of boreal forests remains highly uncertain. A growing body of evidence indicates that boreal forests are shifting toward being a net carbon dioxide source due to increases in soil respiration. To offset this loss of carbon, ecosystems rely on sustained vegetation uptake and accumulation of carbon through plant photosynthesis. However, it is unclear how environmental conditions, particularly moisture and temperature, affect the timing, duration and magnitude of photosynthetic carbon uptake (i.e., photosynthetic phenology) across boreal plant functional types. To address these important knowledge gaps, this study focuses on a leaf-to-watershed analysis at the Caribou-Poker Creek (BONA) Watershed in Alaska. Specifically, the study seeks to answer the question, “What are the environmental and biological controls of photosynthetic phenology in permafrost-affected boreal forests?” This research will provide training to undergraduate and graduate students in field and laboratory research practices. The project will also partner with science educators within the PolarTREC program to develop informational StoryMaps, educational videos, and learning activities to raise public awareness of the important ecosystem services that boreal forests provide to society.  

This study will use a novel approach that incorporates high-frequency observations of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) as an indicator of vegetation gross primary productivity (GPP), and L-band microwave backscattering intensity as an indicator of canopy water content. These measurements will be complemented by a suite of observations including leaf and ecosystem gas exchange, and environmental measurements (e.g., soil temperature, soil moisture, water flow velocity) along a soil-to-vegetation continuum. The observation will be used to identify the key functional relationships between GPP and environmental conditions occurring at the stand and watershed levels through statistical analyses (e.g., multivariate adaptive regression splines). Newly gained insight will be used to optimize a data and process-model integration framework using the remote-sensing driven CARbon Data Model (CARDAMOM) and to extend from the BONA watershed to the boreal forests of Alaska and northwestern Canada. The CARDAMOM framework will allow us to: (1) obtain new, observation-constrained, regional estimates of GPP; (2) assess the regional sensitivity of boreal carbon dioxide uptake under various climate scenarios; and (3) identify the sink potential and trajectory of GPP in boreal forests, given the state of climate warming, a lengthening growing season, and changes in soil water conditions. The study results will be an important step forward in reducing uncertainty in GPP budget estimates for boreal forests, and will help set priorities for future model improvements. 

This project is co-funded by the OPP Arctic Natural Sciences Program and DEB Ecosystem Science Program.

projectOutComesReport:
The boreal forests have been going through important changes as a result of the changing external factors. The productivity of boreal forests is influenced by a myriad of environmental and biological drivers, and their relative contribution changes throughout the season. Understanding how boreal forests respond to the changing environment is essential to predicting how the boreal landscape will look in the future. 

Our project aimed to better understand the environmental and biological controls of photosynthetic phenology in the permafrost-affected boreal forests of North America, and identify how these controls influence the net CO2 exchange status (i.e., carbon flux budgets) of boreal forests.  To address our overarching goals, we focused on the Caribou-Poker Creek Research (BONA) watershed in Interior Alaska. We installed a new, integrated forest monitoring system that spanned from the  National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) tower to an upland tower installed through this project in partnership with NEON.

Our integrated monitoring system, which operated from 2021 through summer 2024, included information from the NEON flux airshed. We installed new instruments to monitor canopy radiance, solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), and L-band microwave backscattering (to identify changing forest water content). We also installed three small-tower (2 m) continuous monitoring stations for microwave backscatter, meteorology, and soil temperature and moisture. In addition to the continuous environmental monitoring sites, we collected observations of belowground CO2 flux and environmental conditions (e.g., soil temperature, soil moisture, soil thaw depth) on a weekly basis from May through September. Our project’s data, in conjunction with ongoing data collected by NEON, is providing new insights into how environmental conditions within a boreal forest interact to influence photosynthetic phenology and seasonal-to-annual carbon flux budgets, and how these differ according to landscape location (e.g., upland vs. lowland) and species (i.e., black spruce vs. birch). Our study is novel because of the very integrated and cross-disciplinary approach, the new state-of-art technology used for SIF monitoring, and innovative applications of L-band microwave to monitor ecosystem water storage/flux. 

Using the integrated remote sensing system, we identified key biological and environmental drivers of photosynthetic activity at the leaf level. At the seasonal level, temperature was by far the most critical driver at the spruce site, followed by needle characteristics and radiation. Whereas the daily response was most influenced by radiation and needle placement. The relationship between fluorescence and photosynthesis follows a pattern that can be well characterized, and during most of the daytime, the relationship between fluorescence yield and photosynthetic yield is positive. We found that SIF tracks the seasonal and diurnal variability of photosynthetic activities in both evergreen and deciduous stands. 

We linked what we observed at the canopy level to the leaf-level activities, providing essential mechanistic understanding to upscale our findings to other boreal forested ecosystems. The ground-based remote sensing observations provide important empirical and theoretical validation to current and future satellite missions.

Through this project, we have provided multi-year support and mentoring to graduate students and undergraduate students at the University of Virginia. Our team worked with teachers from the PolarTrec as part of our outreach program. In addition ,we worked with an artist to create photography exhibitions of various types of boreal vegetation.
