abstractText:
This award is supported by the Major Research Instrumentation and the Chemistry Research Instrumentation programs. The University of Virginia (UVA) is acquiring a single crystal X-ray diffractometer to support Professor Robert Gilliard and colleagues: Thomas Gunnoe and Diane Dickie. In general, an X-ray diffractometer allows accurate and precise measurements of the full three-dimensional structure of a molecule, including bond distances and angles.  It provides accurate information about the spatial arrangement of a molecule relative to neighboring molecules. The studies described here impact many areas, including organic and inorganic chemistry, materials chemistry and biochemistry. This instrument is an integral part of teaching as well as research and research training of undergraduate and graduate students in chemistry and biochemistry as well as other engineering fields at this institution. In addition, the diffractometer has broad impact on teaching and training, outreach activities, and undergraduate research at UVA. The regional partners from primarily undergraduate institutions (PUIs) have significant female and underrepresented minority populations the also benefit from the use of this instrumentation.

The award of the X-ray diffractometer is aimed at enhancing research and education at all levels. The instrument acquisition impacts the characterization of synthetic inorganic and organic materials useful to advance manufacturing. The instrumentation is used for studying catalytic processes and using electrochemistry to generate energy relevant products, e.g., conversion of low potential energy chemicals into high energy chemicals for the scaled use of renewable energy sources such as wind, solar. In addition, the diffractometer benefits the exploration of materials chemistry and engineering. It is also used to characterize products relevant to biological chemistry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The Bruker D8 Venture micro-focus dual source single crystal X-ray diffractometer with a PhotonIII detector was installed in late March 2021. Single crystal X-ray diffractometers are primarily used to determine the 3-D structure of new molecules created by synthetic chemists. Knowing the structure of a molecule is the first step towards understanding the properties of the molecule. The molecules that have been studied with our diffractometer may someday be used as new medicines or new catalysts for green energy development. They are also molecules that simply help us discover the basic rules of how atoms connect to one another. 

After less than three years of operation, data collected on this diffractometer has already appeared in 40 peer-reviewed journal articles. Other research output includes at least 19 oral and/or poster presentation at local, regional, national and international conferences, 4 Ph.D. dissertations, and 9 non-peer-reviewed depositions to the Cambridge Structural Database. The main users of the diffractometer come from the University of Virginia's Department of Chemistry, with 53 students and postdocs from 8 different labs having submitted research samples for diffraction studies. Approximately half of them are fully or partially trained to collect data independently. The diffractometer also serves a large number of researchers outside of the chemistry department. It has attracted users from 16 different groups in the UVA departments of Physics, Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Materials Science, and from the School of Medicine. Finally, we have users from 11 other universities in Virginia, Georgia, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, and one start-up business in Virginia.

The diffractometer is also a crucial component of the university's teaching mission. In particular, a graduate-level class in X-ray crystallography, CHEM 5380 – Determination of Molecular Structure by Diffraction Methods. This class has been offered four times since the installation of the diffractometer, serving 58 undergraduate and graduate students. All have had multiple hand-on experiences with the diffractometer. The diffractometer is also featured in annual visits to the X-ray diffraction lab by students from the UVA Environmental Sciences department  Geochemistry (EVGE 5850) and Isotope Geochemistry (EVGE 5860) classes. There is also an ongoing collaboration with Clark University’s CHEM 250 class (Inorganic Chemistry) wherein the students send samples by mail to be run on the diffractometer with one data collection done live on Zoom for them to see.

title: MRI: Acquisition of a Single Crystal X-ray Diffractometer at the University of Virginia

abstractText:
These astronomers seek to understand what causes clouds of gas in space to collapse to form stars.  The immediate cause is the force of gravity, but why gravity acts quickly on some clouds and slowly in others remains a puzzle.  The investigators have a plan to solve this puzzle by using detailed observations of gas clouds located in two nearby satellite galaxies, the Magellanic Clouds. The observations, taken with NSF’s Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array’s (ALMA) observatory, will have the quality and detail needed to measure the properties of the gas.  The investigators will compare measurements of the stellar environment with the locations and ages of young stars.  The investigators are from three different universities, and each will contribute to training of next generation scientists. The students will get hands-on experience in the techniques of scientific data analysis and instrumentation.  The team will develop of new virtual reality tools for improving the public understanding of science.

With the ALMA’s unprecedented sensitivity and access to the southern sky, astronomers are beginning to resolve the clumpy, filamentary structure of molecular clouds in the Magellanic Clouds. Analysis has shown that the velocity dispersion of the molecular gas at a given scale increases with the overall star formation activity of the cloud, suggesting that energetic feedback from young stars plays a significant role in maintaining turbulent motions within the cloud.  However, other lines of evidence, including our finding that clumps and filaments are typically marginally unstable to collapse, support the view that increased velocity dispersion and star formation can both be driven by gravitational instability.  The investigators plan observations to reveal the conditions for star formation.  They will use a broad, survey-based, approach which can identify regions deficient in one of the key ingredients (e.g., young stars or dense gas) and thus more accurately distinguish cause and effect.  Combining ALMA imaging of the molecular gas on sub-parsec scales with infrared surveys of the young stellar populations in these galaxies will provide new insights into the roles of triggering, feedback, and cloud conditions in the star formation process.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Stars form from dense gas in galaxies.  How many stars form, of what size, and at what rate, in different parts of a galaxy determine how that galaxy will evolve and change over cosmic time, so it is important to understand these outcomes.  Once formed, stars heat, ionize, and energize their natal clouds, enhancing or suppressing further star formation, depending on the detailed physical conditions.  Studying this physics requires resolving structures smaller than a few light years, which even with modern telescopes can only beaccomplished in our nearest neighbor galaxies.

This award funded a comprehensive study in our nearest large neighbor galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We combined new measurements of dense interstellar gas from the Atacama Large (sub)Millimeter Array with infrared measurements of the newly forming stars to analyze star formation and feedback.  The LMC contains the nearest site of extremely concentrated star formation, the super-star cluster R136 in the Tarantula Nebula 30 Doradus. Figure 1 shows the filamentary structure of molecular gas traced by CO emission. We analyzed newly forming stars stars in the region and determined their masses and amount of circumstellar dust (a measure of their age, as they emerge from their formation cocoons). Our analysis showed that although the gas near R136 has elevated kinetic energy, it is no less likely to collapse and form new stars than more distant gas - i.e. the existing extreme star formation destroys molecules and clears more diffuse gas, but may not be able to prevent already-dense clumps from forming new stars.  We used formaldehyde emission to measure the gas temperature in the region, finding again that although the star cluster heats the outsides of nearby clumps, that may not be enough to stop those clumps from forming new stars.

We performed similar analyses of several regions in the LMC, spanning the range of star formation intensity from the very intense 30 Doradus down to very quiescent molecular clouds, which are barely forming any massive stars at all, despite having as much or more dense gas than 30 Doradus.  Figure 3 shows how nu0, a measure of how much kinetic energy is present in the gas relative to gravitational energy at a given surface density, increases with increasing levels of 3 tracers of star formation activity.  Quantifying such relationships is very important: although modern astrophysical numerical simulations are powerful enough to calculate the time evolution of entire galaxies, they usually use an assumed prescription for star formation feedback. It is thus essential to actually measure the feedback relations directly using observations of nearby galaxies such as in the work funded by this award.

Astronomy has tremendous power to attract students and non-scientists to learn science, because images of space are beautiful and mysterious, and because of the fundamental human desire to understand the cosmos and our place in it.  Understanding astronomy more deeply than the pretty images, and using it as a gateway to helping people learn science, does often require mental manipulation of three dimensional structures, and it is well known that such concepts can be challenging to learn. For example, many students have difficulty understanding the phases of the moon because of a poor mental model of the motions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun in three dimensional space.  Immersive technology like Virtual Reality (VR) is very powerful to help people intuitively understand complex 3d objects.  This award funded the development of a VR educational module, which used the scientific ALMA data of 30 Doradus, along with a numerical simulation of a planet-forming disk of dense gas around a young star, and other astronomical images.   The participant can "walk" around the ALMA telescope, learn how that instrument works, can fly to 30 Doradus and around the star forming molecular cloud learning where the stars form, and zoom into the planet-forming disk.  We created guidance, activity, and assessment materials for teachers, aiming the activity at middle school to early college levels.  Figure 2 shows a snapshot from inside the VR module.

abstractText:
Populations of organisms located in different, often far-apart places can change over time in similar ways. This natural phenomenon, known as synchrony, is critical to the persistence, stability, and resilience of plant and animal populations, and can have cascading effects on biodiversity, ecosystem function, and associated benefits to society. However, many aspects of synchrony are poorly resolved. For example, understanding the influence of multiple drivers of synchrony—such as climatic events and predators—has been a longstanding challenge in ecology. Moreover, the causes of synchrony may change over space, time, and timescale (e.g., annual vs. decadal synchrony), but this possibility is rarely explored, especially in marine ecosystems. The consequences of synchrony for the dynamics of diverse ecological communities, and the potential for synchrony to have cascading effects across ecosystem boundaries (e.g., from sea to land), are also understudied. Addressing these gaps is especially pressing because growing evidence indicates that climate change may alter patterns of synchrony, which could lead to diminished spatial resilience of ecosystems. This project studies coastal kelp forests and sandy beach ecosystems to address several current gaps in the understanding of synchrony. The project is generating knowledge to improve the understanding of these economically-valuable environments and the many organisms that they sustain. Broader impacts extend through the mentorship of researchers across career stages and student training in coastal ecology and data science. To improve educational opportunities for students from groups underrepresented in science, the project is creating a Coastal-Heartland Marine Biology Exchange, in which undergraduates from the Midwest travel to California to carry out coastal field research, and undergraduates from Los Angeles interested in marine biology travel to Kansas to learn biostatistics. To benefit the management of kelp forests in California that have suffered dramatic declines in recent years, workshops are being hosted with coastal managers, conservation practitioners, and other stakeholders to identify restoration sites to enhance regional recovery, stability, and resilience. Methods, software, and data that are useable across scientific disciplines are published online following reproducible and transparent standards.

The objective of this project is to investigate the patterns and causes of synchrony in giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) forests and the consequences for coastal ecosystem structure and function. By integrating and leveraging numerous long-term, large-scale datasets and analyzing them with new statistical techniques, the investigators are assessing how oceanographic conditions, propagule dispersal, and sea urchin herbivory interact to structure the synchrony and stability of giant kelp populations over the past 36 years across 10 degrees of latitude in the northeast Pacific Ocean. New wavelet modeling tools and other statistical techniques are used to quantify the drivers of synchrony and how they operate across geography, time, and timescales. Using a 20-year spatial timeseries of reef biodiversity, it will be determined how giant kelp and other factors induce synchrony in a speciose community of understory algae through ‘cascades of synchrony’ Moreover, the team is testing the degree to which giant kelp synchrony propagates across ecosystem boundaries to sandy beaches through the transport and deposition of allochthonous organic matter (kelp wrack), and how such spatial subsidies produce bottom-up cascades of synchrony to beach invertebrates and shorebirds.

projectOutComesReport:
This project investigated a remarkable and ubiquitous natural phenomenon called synchrony, in which populations of plants or animals in different places fluctuate in similar ways over time, even if very far apart. Synchrony can influence the stability of ecosystems at local to regional scales, and the biodiversity they sustain. The research focused on synchrony in giant kelp forests—towering underwater habitats found along the west coast of North America and many other regions worldwide—and examined how these dynamics affect coastal biodiversity and ecological resilience.

Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) is the largest of all algae and among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth. Its forests provide essential habitat for hundreds of marine species and support industries including kelp harvest, commercial and recreational fisheries, and coastal tourism. However, kelp forests are increasingly affected by changes in ocean conditions—such as shifts in temperature, storm patterns, and food webs. This project set out to understand how synchrony in kelp populations arises, what drives it, and how it shapes broader ecological dynamics—from rocky reefs to sandy beaches.

The research team used 40 years of satellite imagery, 20 years of field survey data, and new cutting-edge statistical tools to analyze synchrony across a broad stretch of coastline from Baja California, Mexico, to Northern California, USA. They found that kelp forests separated by hundreds of miles are synchronous with one another. This synchrony is shaped by a combination of factors, including wave disturbance, nutrient availability, and the dispersal of kelp spores among sites via ocean currents. This last discovery offered the first clear evidence that dispersal can synchronize populations of marine organisms across large distances, challenging previous assumptions that synchrony in the sea is driven only by environmental forces.

The researchers also found that synchrony plays out over multiple timescales—from seasonal cycles to multi-decade patterns—and that large-scale environmental variation can drive these changes. One study showed that warming conditions can shift the tipping points at which kelp forests transition to alternative ecosystem states, providing new insight into the conditions under which these ecosystems are most vulnerable.

Beyond kelp itself, the project examined how synchrony spreads across ecological communities. The researchers found that understory algae—seaweeds that grow beneath the kelp canopy—tend to mirror the ups and downs of kelp. Disturbance by storm-driven waves caused cascades of synchrony across species competing for light near the seafloor, providing rare empirical evidence for what drives patterns of biodiversity across geographic space.

The work extended to adjacent ecosystems as well. The team studied how floating kelp detritus (wrack) washes ashore and supports shorebird populations, which feed on small invertebrates living in the wrack. Thus, synchrony in kelp biomass cascades to synchronize aggregations of predatory shorebirds, some of which are threatened or endangered. This cross-boundary connection means that fluctuations in kelp production at sea can influence bird foraging patterns on beaches, highlighting the broad ecological reach of synchrony.

To support these and other discoveries, the team developed open-access tools to enhance scientific research and decision-making. The KelpWatch.org platform now offers public access to decades of satellite-based kelp canopy biomass data throughout the world. The project also developed wsyn, an R software package for analyzing ecological time series, which has been downloaded over 15,000 times globally.

The project made a strong contribution to education and workforce development. A central initiative was the Coastal-Heartland Marine Biology Exchange, a training program that brought together undergraduate students from the US Midwest and coastal states. Participants received field training in marine science, mentoring in data analysis and scientific communication, and presented their work at national conferences. Several students have since launched careers in environmental science, industry, and policy.

In total, the project supported more than a dozen graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, many of whom went on to careers in research, education, and coastal conservation and management across academic, governmental, and nonprofit sectors. Research findings have informed natural resource management decisions by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and The Nature Conservancy, helping guide actions such as kelp harvest regulation and habitat restoration.

The project produced over twenty peer-reviewed publications, including several in leading journals such as PNAS, Ecology Letters, and Nature Ecology & Evolution. These contributions have shaped scientific understanding of ecosystem dynamics and inspired new research on synchrony in both marine and terrestrial systems.

By uncovering the patterns that connect ecosystems across time and space, this project has expanded the scientific understanding of synchrony and developed new tools to support the stewardship of ecologically and economically important coastal environments.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is to explore applications of new wirelessly connected sensors.  The proposed technology advances a an ultra-low-power sensor device for the Internet of Things (IoT), smart dust, or edge intelligence (EI) devices. Relative to current sensors, the proposed technology may create 100-fold improvements in the cost of thorough coverage and battery life, virtually eliminating the cost of battery replacement and sensor maintenance. Example applications in agriculture include preventive, cost-effective, and continuous monitoring of temperature, rainfall, wind direction, soil moisture, pests, and illness for informed decision-making.  Other applications may include preventive/therapeutic healthcare, animal welfare, environmental monitoring, transportation, and industrial monitoring.

This I-Corps project investigates translation of a novel system-on-chip (SoC) with end-to-end computing on asynchronous streams data-path that is composed of Asynchronous Sigma-Delta Modulators (ASDM) for acquiring sensor data, a computing-core for streams, a clock-less wireless interface and an analog memory. The key for the SoC power efficiency is the unique data representation - the ASDM maps analog data to asynchronous streams of 1s and 0s instead of digital numbers. The streams are sent to the computing-core composed of processing elements, such as multipliers and adders. A multiplier for streams may be implemented with a single AND gate and an adder with a 2:1 multiplexer, achieving savings in power and area of up to 90% compared with typical approaches.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Outcomes Report: CleverMote - NSF I-Corps Program.

Intellectual Merit: The CleverMote project, conducted under the NSF I-Corps program, has made significant contributions to the intellectual merit of scientific and technological knowledge in the following ways:

Technological Advancement: The CleverMote project initially aimed to develop an innovative system-on-chip (SoC) design for edge-intelligence devices based on Asynchronous Stream Processing principles. However, through rigorous customer discovery interviews conducted during the early stages of the project, valuable insights were gained. As a result, a pivot was made, and the project shifted its focus towards computational RFID technology for low-power sensing nodes. This pivot demonstrated the team's ability to adapt and align the project with market demands, leading to novel technological advancements in low-power sensing and edge computing.

Innovative System Design: The CleverMote project successfully developed a Computational RFID IoT system for applications such as Smart Cities/Buildings and Preventive Maintenance/Industry 4.0. Technical advances were made on the design of a custom RFID reader based on a COTS platform from ST Micro, an innovative CRFID tag using a special metal-compatible RF patch antenna and a flexible Pseudo-Battery-Assisted-Passive RFID scheme that achieves the high sensitivity of battery operated tags while still being batteryless. This is achieved by having a secondary energy harvesting path with a long duty cycle that charges a capacitor which acts as the ?Pseudo-Battery.? The research conducted during this project has expanded the knowledge base of low-power sensing and computing, contributing to advancements in the field.

Broader Impacts: The CleverMote project has the potential to create broader impacts on society and the economy through the following means:

Commercialization Potential: The pivot made early in the project, driven by customer discovery interviews, has significantly enhanced the commercialization potential of CleverMote. By aligning the technology with market demands and focusing on edge-intelligence devices, CleverMote has the potential for widespread adoption in markets such as healthcare, and industrial monitoring. The project's outcomes have paved the way for potential partnerships, licensing agreements, and spin-off ventures that can drive economic growth and job creation.

Societal Benefits: The CleverMote technology has the potential to bring about significant societal benefits. By enabling preventive, cost-effective, and continuous monitoring of key factors in various applications, such as temperature, vibration, CleverMote can empower decision-makers to take immediate action during unexpected events or dangerous situations. This technology can lead to improved resource utilization, reduced waste, and enhanced safety measures in sectors such as industry, environmental monitoring, and healthcare.

Workforce Development and Education: The CleverMote project has fostered workforce development and education in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Through their participation in the NSF I-Corps program, the team members, including technical lead Professor Mircea R. Stan and entrepreneurial lead Tommy J. Tracy II, have gained valuable entrepreneurial skills and experiences. These experiences not only enhance their professional growth but also inspire and motivate students in STEM fields, contributing to the development of a skilled workforce.

Collaboration and Partnerships: The CleverMote project has facilitated collaborations with industry partners and stakeholders in various sectors. The customer discovery interviews conducted during the early stages of the project allowed for valuable insights and feedback, fostering connections with potential end-users and customers. These collaborations and partnerships will play a crucial role in the successful translation of CleverMote into real-world applications, ensuring that the developed technology meets market needs and achieves maximum societal impact.

In conclusion, the CleverMote project, conducted under the NSF I-Corps program, has made significant contributions to intellectual merit and broader impacts. Through the pivot made early in the project based on customer discovery interviews, the team demonstrated their ability to adapt and align their technology with market demands, resulting in the development of an innovative CRFID design for edge-intelligence devices. The project has advanced the knowledge base in low-power sensing and computing paving the way for future research and development.

abstractText:
There are numerous forms of flight ranging from the natural flapping of insect wings to engineered multi-rotor helicopters. Among the diversity of systems for producing flight forces, the flying snake embodies a highly unexpected and non-intuitive solution for aerial locomotion. With a cylindrical body, the snake has no extendable surfaces to create or control flight forces. Despite these limitations, the Asian arboreal species known as ‘flying’ snakes possess a surprisingly sophisticated ability to glide. These snakes jump from trees, flatten their body, and undulate in the air in a complex three-dimensional pattern to produce aerial locomotion. Most surprisingly, the snakes can actively maneuver in the air, capable of turning in mid-air under their own volition. Understanding how flying snakes achieve such feats is the first step toward duplicating this behavior in engineered devices, which could significantly advance design of robots in complex environments, with important applications to surveillance, search-and-rescue, and disaster monitoring.
 
The aerial interaction physics of flying snakes - the strong coupling between the translational and rotational degrees of freedom of the snake as an articulated body - is largely unknown. This project will test the hypothesis that translational-rotational coupling is achieved through feedback between self-deformations (driven by undulation) and unsteady fluid mechanics. The research will use a combination of animal observations, experimental fluid mechanics, and computational fluid dynamics to reveal the fluid mechanics of deforming articulated bodies, of which the flying snake (genus Chrysopelea) is the prime example. The application of adaptive mesh refinement-based immersed boundary method to study fluid flows produced by gliding snakes will enable more efficient investigations on other complex fluids problems with dynamically moving objects across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. The proposed experimental and computational framework can potentially re-define the form and function of locomotion in fluid media for aerial and underwater robotic systems with enhanced mobility. The project involves a broad participation plan that will benefit a diverse range of groups. The principal investigators will engage under-represented students through programmatic connections to regional HBCUs, for summer undergraduate research as well as recruiting of graduate research assistants, at the three collaborating universities. Flying snakes excite the imagination of both students and the public, and the results of the experiments and computations will be disseminated both professionally and publicly, to media outlets and also directly to the public through social media.

projectOutComesReport:
Flying snakes are among the few animals capable of controlled gliding flight despite lacking wings. This research investigated the aerodynamic mechanisms that enable these snakes to glide efficiently by undulating their bodies in midair. By using advanced computational simulations, we explored how the body’s motion and shape influence airflow, lift generation, and overall flight stability. The findings contribute to fundamental aerodynamics, bio-inspired robotics, and a broader understanding of animal locomotion.

 Intellectual Merit

The project focused on uncovering the aerodynamic principles underlying flying snake locomotion, particularly how undulation and body shape influence flight performance. Using high-fidelity numerical simulations, we identified key mechanisms that enhance lift and stability, including the role of body-generated vortices and the effects of vertical and horizontal bending during gliding.

Key findings include:

  • Vortex Dynamics and Lift Enhancement: Flying snakes generate leading-edge vortices through body motion, which help sustain lift. Small vertical bending movements optimize lift, while excessive bending reduces performance.
  • Head-Body Interaction in Aerodynamics: The snake’s head movement influences airflow over the body, enhancing lift and improving overall gliding efficiency. The backward-facing step flow condition created by the head-body shape supports stronger vortex formation.
  • Tandem Airfoil Effects: The interactions between different parts of the snake’s body improve aerodynamic efficiency. Aligning the rear body section with the airflow from the front reduces drag and enhances the lift-to-drag ratio, optimizing gliding performance.

Broader Impacts

This study has broader implications beyond aerodynamics, influencing fields such as biology, robotics, and fluid mechanics:

  • Biology and Animal Locomotion: The research contributes to the study of gliding animals by providing a detailed analysis of how shape adaptation and undulatory movement enhance flight performance. These insights improve our understanding of animal biomechanics and evolutionary adaptations.
  • Bio-Inspired Robotics and Engineering: The findings offer valuable design principles for soft robotics and autonomous flying systems. Inspired by the flying snake’s efficient movement, engineers can develop reconfigurable UAVs and shape-adaptive aerial vehicles capable of maneuvering in complex environments.
  • Computational Methods for Fluid Dynamics: The project developed and refined high-resolution computational techniques for simulating unsteady flow around deformable bodies. These methods can be applied to various engineering problems, including aircraft design, underwater robotics, and energy-efficient propulsion systems.

Summary

This project significantly advanced our understanding of flying snake aerodynamics by revealing how body motion influences airflow and lift generation. The discoveries have practical applications in robotics, biomechanics, and engineering, paving the way for new innovations in aerial mobility. By bridging biology and engineering, this research not only deepens our knowledge of animal flight but also inspires new approaches to designing adaptive and efficient flying systems.

abstractText:
The ever-increasing demand for wireless communications has created a need for extremely wideband radio transmitters that can deliver multi-giga-bit-per-second data rates to individual users. A promising approach that can enable these high data rates and even future faster tera-bit-per-second (Tbps) data rate is the use of the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) spectrum (30 to 300 GHz) which readily provides a vast amount of bandwidth. Cellular networks operating at mm-wave frequencies will increase the required base station bandwidth significantly, but they will also decrease the size of each cell dramatically due to the large path loss and atmospheric absorption at these frequencies. As a result, installing a base station on every light pole may become necessary to guarantee coverage in an urban environment. This scenario creates many technical challenges since the baseband rack-mount hardware equipment cannot be placed adjacent to each antenna in this case. To address this, solutions are needed that allow for dense deployment of compact mm-wave base stations with Tbps-level throughput whose complex communication equipment can be placed away from the antenna itself. Compared to pure electronic solutions, photonic technologies offer many technical advantages to realize such wideband systems. However, traditional photonic approaches are not scalable and suffer from large insertion loss and large footprint when cascading discrete components. This project will address these challenges by a joint multidisciplinary effort that leverages recent developments in nonlinear optics, integrated photonics, and wideband integrated antennas to enable a compact platform that can provide a vast array of wireless channels with over 1 Tbps data capacity.
   
This project aims to develop a new paradigm for chip-scale Tbps wireless systems. The approach is based on optical dual-microresonators with ultra-high quality factor, where mode-locked femtosecond soliton pulses are generated through the balance between cavity dispersion and Kerr nonlinearity to create arrays of stable optical carriers. Filtering, data modulation, and multiplexing will be accomplished in the optical domain through ring resonators, heterogeneously integrated high-bitrate modulators, and arrayed waveguide gratings. Conversion into the mm-wave frequencies will be achieved by heterodyne detection in ultra-wideband photodetectors, which will be co-designed with integrated antennas to ensure efficient radiation into free space. This effort is expected to advance not only the performance of individual components and circuits, but also the miniaturization and applicability of integrated photonic-electronic technologies to push the state-of-the-art for mm-wave wireless communications. The fact that all key components will be integrated on a single chip will pave the way toward manufacturable large-scale mm-wave photonic integrated circuits with small size, light weight, and low power, which will also benefit other applications in sensing and imaging. The research will allow in-depth studies of the potential benefits, trade-offs, and limits of photonically driven high-frequency technologies.

projectOutComesReport:
To meet the growing demand for wideband communications, next-generation wireless systems that can deliver terabit-per-second (Tbps) data rates at mm-wave frequencies beyond 100 GHz are of increasing interest. Purely electronic approaches face fundamental limitations at these frequencies, while photonic technologies offer intrinsic broadband capability, parallelism, and high-speed modulation and detection. However, existing photonic solutions are often bulky and impractical due to reliance on discrete components.

In this project we developed a novel photonic approach for chip-scale, high-capacity wireless communication systems based on optical microresonators generating soliton frequency combs (microcombs), i.e. ultra-stable, evenly spaced optical signals, from which pure millimeter-wave (mm-wave) signals are derived using integrated high-power, high-speed photodiodes. We demonstrated that microcombs, together with photonic integrated modulators, filters, and high-speed photodetectors, can serve as essential devices for multi-channel communication systems. Using single and dual microcomb systems, we generated and controlled multi-channel microwave signals, enabling arbitrary waveform synthesis and achieving one of the lowest phase noise levels reported for a 100 GHz photonically generated signal by using optical frequency division (OFD). For stabilizing the millimeter wave signals, we found that a Kerr OFD approach is much simpler to implement compared to traditional methods. Comparative analysis showed that, under identical biasing conditions, the soliton microcomb approach produced 10 mW output power, exceeding the efficiency and power scaling of conventional two-laser heterodyne techniques. We also achieved the first on-chip integration of soliton microcombs with high-bandwidth photodiodes, delivering compact, low-noise mm-wave generation on a silicon photonics platform. The heterogeneously integrated photodiodes reached  0.76 A/W responsivity and high output power at 100 GHz.

In parallel, we designed, fabricated, and tested discrete GaAsSb/InP photodiodes utilizing type II band alignment. We showed that this approach is suitable for detecting signals up to 325 GHz. To stabilize the laser sources in our system, we developed a compact heterogeneously integrated optical phase-locked loop for frequency difference locking. We designed and integrated optical filters and modulators on silicon-on-insulator chips, and successfully demonstrated a multi-channel transmitter with gigabit-per-second data rates operating at microwave frequencies.

By integrating chip-scale soliton generation, photodetection, and high-speed modulation, this project established a scalable path toward manufacturable mm-wave transmitters in silicon photonics. The resulting technologies, ultra-low-phase-noise photonically driven mm-wave sources, high-bandwidth integrated photodiodes, and dual-comb waveform synthesis, are applicable to next-generation communication networks and represent an advancement of CMOS-compatible integrated photonics-electronics technologies.

abstractText:
This project aims to discover new ways of controlling how electrons move across arrays of quantum dots by using light as a switch. Quantum dots are nanoparticles of semiconductors with optical and electrical properties that can be tuned through changing the size of the particles. This research is focused on studying how flow of electrons between neighboring quantum dots can be turned ‘on’ and ‘off’ by switching the shape of molecules connecting the quantum dots using light with different colors. Such phenomena can be exploited to make materials for optically switchable components for optical computing and memory devices that are faster and more efficient compared to traditional electronics. Broadly, this research has a potential to advance the fundamental understanding of nanoscale charge transfer which is crucial for understanding optical and electrical processes in macromolecular, nanoscale, and biological systems. The research activities are integrated with educational efforts aimed at enhancing the recruitment, training, and retention of students in the science and engineering fields, especially among underrepresented groups at the University of Virginia and Old Dominion University. With an emphasis on middle and high school students, hands-on activities on 'Switching Molecules with Light' are provided. Undergraduate researchers are recruited through the Virginia-North Carolina Alliance for Minority Participation and other programs.

The proposed research aims to test a hypothesis that the rates of charge transfer and exciton dissociation in colloidal quantum dot assemblies can be modulated by changing conformation of the 'bridge' photochromic molecules that inter-connect the quantum dots. To this end, a combination of nanoparticle synthesis, organic synthesis, surface chemistry characterization, optical spectroscopy, electrical measurements and X-ray scattering is employed. In the context of Marcus theory, the impact of potential barrier height on nanoscale charge transfer is systematically studied while keeping exactly the same charge donor-acceptor pair and the surface chemistry at contacts. This research has a potential to result in the discovery of a novel class of quantum dot assemblies with optically switchable light emission and non-volatile ‘read’ and ‘write’ operations. The dense, fast and reliable on-chip compatible non-volatile optical memory materials potentially obtained through this research can lead to new research directions and capabilities for optical computing, data storage, processing and transmission. The research team from the two universities will (1) determine the relationship between the potential barrier height and the rates of charge transfer and exciton dissociation in quantum dot assemblies in the context of Marcus theory, (2) investigate the relationship between bridge molecule structure and functional groups on charge transfer and exciton dissociation in quantum dot assemblies, and (3) demonstrate quantum dot assemblies with optically switchable photoluminescence intensity.

projectOutComesReport:
This project tested a hypothesis that the rates of charge transfer and exciton dissociation in colloidal quantum dot (CQD) assemblies can be modulated by changing conformation of the 'bridge' molecules that inter-connect CQDs. The project achieved three major scientific goals: (1) determine the relationship between the potential barrier height and the rates of charge transfer and exciton dissociation in CQD assemblies in the context of Marcus theory, (2) investigate the relationship between bridge molecule structure and functional groups on charge transfer and exciton dissociation in CQD assemblies, and (3) demonstrate CQD assemblies with optically switchable photoluminescence intensity. Our results were published in five peer-reviewed journal papers and they show that lowering the inter-CQD potential barrier height increases the exciton delocalization and dissociation through tunneling. To the best of our knowledge, this project was the first to investigate the impact of bridge molecule configuration on exciton dynamics all with identical donor-acceptor CQD pairs.

In addition to achieving the scientific goals, providing training to students at different levels was a major educational goal of this project. Throught this project, two graduate students and two undergraduate students have received training in research fields of optical and electrical materials. Both graduate students have successfully graduated with Ph.D. degrees. The research team also provided outreach activities to underrepresented minority students in middle schools of Starr Hill area in Charlottesville. The "Exciting molecules with light" activities engaged the middle school students in topics such as electromagnetic spectrum, exciting molecules with microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet light. During the activities, students built and tested their own solar cells based on molecules from blackberries.

In terms of potential impact on technology transfer, the switchable photoluminescence intensity from CQDs demonstrated in this project can provide unique opportunities for optical memory and computing technologies. The major challenges facing the current state-of-the-art non-volatile on-chip compatible optical memory materials, such as phase change materials and photochromic molecules, are that phase change materials require large energy light excitations to induce melting and photochromic molecules lack non-destructive readout capabilities due to the readout operation itself causing the switch. In contrast, our photochromic molecule bridged CQD assemblies exhibit near-infrared light emission that can be increased or decreased with ultraviolet and visible light exposure. In other words, the “read” operations can be performed all in near-infrared region that does not cause flipping of the photochromic molecule configuration. Therefore, the results from this project can lead to solving the challenge of photochromic materials switching their configuration during the “read” operation and provide a new class of materials for non-volatile optical memory and computing applications.

abstractText:
The vision of a smart city is underpinned by its ability to collect, manage, and use data. However, data access remains a fundamental challenge across city agencies, public institutions, and community stakeholders. This project is championing a paradigm shift in data sharing by implementing a new data access framework that allows users to share access to data in-situ instead of sending copies of data around. This project builds on the new data access paradigm to deploy a city Data Access Network (City-DAN) to support city managers get timely access to important data for fast decision and response. City-DAN is piloted first in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam and then scaled to other ASEAN cities.  This activity is in response to NSF Dear Colleague Letter Supporting Transition of Research into Cities through the US ASEAN ((Association of Southeast Asian Nations Cities) Smart Cities Partnership in collaboration with NSF and the US State Department.  The research team (University of Virginia) is working closely with stakeholders in Ho Chi Minh City including city managers, departments, and community organizers as well as Vietnam National University – International University to transition technology into practice.

The proposed distributed, peer-to-peer data access framework represents an ambitious vision of the next generation data ecosystem. This project establishes a foundational data platform to underpin smart cities by addressing issues of data integrity, provenance, control, and timely access. This project takes advantage of the unique deployment opportunity to pursue a vibrant research agenda on grid computing. Specific research areas include advanced cyber infrastructure, cybersecurity, networking, and persistent identifiers. This project will especially focus on identity and access management (IAM) in the context of unreliable infrastructure and weak level-of-assurance (identify proofing) baselines. The project will examine new approaches for enhancing reliability while balancing with transparency and QoS. Lessons learned also can be adopted to advance the smart and connected community research community in the US and other countries.

projectOutComesReport:
Flooding is one of the most pervasive and costly natural hazards facing urban environments worldwide. In rapidly developing regions, such as those across Southeast Asia, weak infrastructure, coupled with high population density and climate volatility, magnifies the frequency and impact of floods. Designed to address this urgent need, our team of researchers have developed a system, reffered to as FloodWatch, set out with a dual purpose: to create a robust, next-generation data-sharing platform capable of collecting and analyzing varied data streams in near real time, and to apply that platform to a high-impact use case of urban flood monitoring and early warning.

To meet its ambitious vision, the project fused multiple technological layers. The research team integrated diverse data sources ranging from weather sensors and crowd-sourced images to time-series data on water levels into a cloud-based analytics pipeline that enables flexible, near-real-time applications. The core intellectual contributions include:

(1) Novel Data Infrastructure and Analytics: Researchers built a modular, globally accessible data infrastructure incorporating IoT devices, machine learning, and an open-ended analytics engine. This framework accelerates scientific exploration of urban flooding through data-driven predictions (e.g., an neural network-based flood severity index) while remaining adaptable for other domains (e.g., air-quality monitoring).

(2)  Automated Validation of Crowd-Sourced Data: A hybrid approach combining a Convolutional Neural Network classifier with real-time weather feeds was developed to validate user-submitted flood images. This innovation extends to other big-data scenarios that require automated content validation.

(3) Multi-City Deployment: FloodWatch was piloted not just in Vietnam (Ho Chi Minh City, Danang, and other sites) but also extended to Charlottesville (USA) and Cote d Azur (France). These testbeds informed technical enhancements to network reliability, data ingestion pipelines, and cross-platform scalability.

(4) Peer-Reviewed Publications & Patent: The project team produced peer-reviewed publications in premier venues (e.g., IEEE, ACM, AAAI) and filed a patent (PCT/US2024/37704) related to the CNN-based flood-image validation system.

An equally significant pillar of FloodWatch is its commitment to community collaboration and capacity-building. Collaborations with local partners in Vietnam, the United States, and France have laid the groundwork for larger-scale adoption, including pilot deployments in multiple cities and ongoing discussions to integrate FloodWatch into official municipal operations. FloodWatch focuses on improving urban resilience to flooding, building international research collaborations, and training a diverse cohort of young scientists and engineers. This collaborative approach led to broader impacts on multiple aspects:

(1) Enhanced Public Safety & Urban Resilience: By delivering near-real-time flood forecasts and risk maps through a user-friendly interface, the system provides actionable information for residents, local governments, and emergency responders, ultimately reducing community vulnerability to floods.

(2) Community Engagement & Cultural Exchange: Collaborations with local maker spaces, municipal agencies (e.g., Danang Intelligent Operations Center), and universities (in Vietnam, the U.S., and Europe) fostered cross-cultural partnerships, including symposiums (ISSCEI) that drew over 80 participants to discuss sustainable urban technologies.

(3) Workforce Development & Student Training: Over the course of the project, dozens of undergraduates and graduate students (from both U.S. and overseas institutions) gained hands-on experience in IoT, data analytics, software engineering, and field deployment. Several graduated to top-tier tech industry roles or prestigious graduate programs, strengthening the global pipeline of STEM talent.

(4) Technology Transfer & Sustainability: Partnerships with the University of Virginia Licensing and Venture Group led to a full patent application and potential commercialization pathways. Ongoing collaborations with international research centers (e.g., the Asian Water Research Center in Ho Chi Minh City) further ensure that FloodWatch remains active, sustainable, and primed for broader adoption across other ASEAN regions and beyond.

Looking forward, FloodWatch trajectory remains promising. Continued expansion through new sensor deployments, deeper integration with municipal dashboards, and enhanced predictive models will refine and extend the platform capabilities. Partnerships with entities like the Asian Water Research Center (CARE) in Ho Chi Minh City and the UVA Licensing and Ventures Group point toward an enduring, multi-stakeholder approach to technology transfer and commercialization. By demonstrating that low-cost sensing, AI-driven data validation, and multi-modal analytics can be integrated into an accessible, globally distributed pipeline, the FloodWatch project paves the way for broader applications that address not just flooding but the complex spectrum of issues confronting modern cities.

abstractText:
Drought is a global and increasingly frequent problem that threatens the vitality of forests and the many benefits they provide to society (including carbon sequestration, timber provisioning, and water cycle regulation). Whether trees thrive or falter during drought depends on how they respond to these stressful conditions. Despite many studies of leaf-level changes to photosynthesis and water use during drought, it is still unclear how trees make integrated and coordinated changes at the scale of the entire plant. For example, trees that change the angles of their leaves can reduce the radiation load at different levels of the canopy, reducing heat stress and water loss. This study investigates the coordinated adjustments of tree canopy structure and physiology under water stress using drought experiments in both growth chambers and in a forest that has a rainfall removal experiment. The investigators bring together traditional measurements of leaf and canopy gas exchange with novel remote sensing techniques that measure canopy structure and physiology. This project will provide interdisciplinary teaching, training, and learning experiences by collaborating with a non-profit organization (Math4Science) that promotes STEM, creating videos of 3D forests, mentoring undergraduate students, and exposing K-12 students from under-represented groups to STEM research.

The degree to which forests will continue to serve as carbon sinks and mitigate climate change hinges on whether trees can make physiological and structural adjustments to cope with changing environmental stressors. Most research to date on tree responses to drought has focused on how trees alter leaf-level physiology, phenology, and carbon mobilization and allocation. However, trees also make structural adjustments in response to drought (e.g., by changing leaf angles) to reduce radiation load and leaf temperature. The work extends current research on plant water use strategies, which is mostly focused on physiological responses at the leaf or ecosystem scales, to a new dimension - canopy structure (leaf angles). The investigators aim to answer the question "To what extent do trees respond to water stress through coordinated adjustments of canopy structure and leaf physiology, and by what mechanisms?" combining measurements of leaf and canopy gas exchange with novel remote sensing techniques that measure canopy structure and leaf physiology, including the Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) and the Unmanned Autonomous Vehicle (UAV). By taking advantage of both classical and novel techniques, this project will provide new insights into the coordination of plant response to water stress over spatial (leaf to canopy) and temporal scales (short to long term). Including mechanical responses in physiological studies of drought at the scales of entire tree crowns will provide novel mechanistic insights into drought-science and will facilitate building comprehensive mechanistic approaches into ecosystem-scale models.

PI Yang (University of Virginia), Co-Is Lerdau (University of Virginia), Novick (Indiana University), Phillips (Indiana University). Grant numbers: IOS-2005574, IOS-2006196.

The degree to which forests will continue to serve as carbon sinks and mitigate climate change

depends on whether trees can make physiological and structural adjustments to cope with changing environmental stressors. This project expands our mechanistic understanding of plant drought response by integrating leaf-level physiological changes with changes in canopy structure, particularly leaf angle changes. Leveraging leaf-level physiological measurements, terrestrial LiDAR, drone-based hyperspectral remote sensing, and field and growth-chamber drought experiments, our work demonstrates and quantifies plants’ physiological and structural responses to drought.

The development of an algorithm to estimate leaf angle from terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data is crucial to the success of our project. We developed an open-source algorithm, TLSLeAF, to extract leaf angle data for hundreds of thousands of leaves in a forest using data collected by TLS. In addition, we developed a drone system that measures solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) and canopy hyperspectral reflectance of individual tree canopies. Leveraging these new techniques, we made novel measurements during our experiments to understand the physiological and structural responses of plants to drought and how those responses are integrated at the whole-plant level.

Our team has conducted both an indoor growth chamber experiment and two outdoor Throughfall Displacement Experiments (TDEs) to understand the mechanistic bases of physiological and structural responses of temperate forests to water stress. During the growth chamber experiment, we measured leaf gas exchange, fluorescence parameters, and leaf angle changes throughout the experiment. We used our TLSLeAF algorithm to quantify leaf angle variations of individual leaves (and the within-leaf variations in leaf surface angle). Our study reveals the mechanisms underlying SIF responses to drought, highlighting that both leaf physiological changes and structural changes result in changes in photosynthesis and SIF, allowing the use of SIF to track drought response at canopy, ecosystem landscape, and continental scales. We tested the canopy scale responses to drought and the use of SIF in our TDEs and were able to show that, with our mechanistic understanding of physiology and structure, we could use SIF to detect drought impacts at the canopy scale. SIF provides a clear signal of drought-induced reductions in carbon uptake.

To understand how leaf traits and canopy structure covary at the sub-continental scale, we sampled leaves of mature trees in Charlottesville, Virginia, and several major NEON sites. We measured leaf angles and key leaf traits of the Leaf Economics Spectrum (LES), including leaf mass per area (LMA) and nitrogen content (N%). These new activities provide a larger dataset than we had originally proposed, which allows us to examine the relationship between leaf angle and other leaf traits across a wide range of ecosystems and landscapes. We found that LMA is negatively correlated with leaf angle across the sites above, demonstrating the importance of incorporating canopy structural traits into the understanding of plant trait strategies.

Our team has trained three graduate students, four undergraduate students, and one postdoctoral researcher. We have hosted high school students from public schools in central Virginia and New York City to demonstrate the use of new technology (e.g., drones) in ecology, and we have worked with an educational non-profit, Math4Science, as they develop science and math curricula.

abstractText:
This grant supports research to develop new knowledge about an electrospray additive manufacturing process to promote the progress of science and to advance national prosperity and well-being by facilitating the manufacture of materials to address water purification challenges and clean water shortages. Electrospray additive manufacturing is a process where organic monomers are deposited onto a surface to form a thin polymer film or membrane. This process carefully controls the way by which these molecules are placed on the surface and can be quickly adapted to manufacture a range of different membrane materials. The electrospray process, in this sense, has significant advantages over conventional film coating or casting processes. An example of one benefit of this approach would be that manufacturers could quickly adapt the process to make tailored water treatment membranes in response to emerging contaminants or pollutants in water. Results from this research benefit the U.S. economy and society by enabling the manufacture of very efficient membranes that provide better access to clean water. This research involves several disciplines including advanced manufacturing, materials science, chemical engineering, and electrochemistry. The use of a multi-disciplinary approach broadens participation of underrepresented groups in research and enhances engineering education and training for the future engineering workforce.

The electrospray additive manufacturing process overcomes fundamental limitations, inherent to conventional manufacturing, that prevent reliable and controlled preparation of very thin polyamide ion exchange membranes with tunable properties. This research addresses knowledge gaps related to the use of electrospray additive manufacturing to enable incorporation of a range of co-monomers into the final membrane. This range of compositions allow the manufacture of materials not previously accessible via conventional manufacturing such as doctor-blade or slot-die casting. The research team prepares and characterizes the membranes to determine if electrospray additive manufacturing can be used to overcome mass transfer, solubility, and reaction kinetics limitations associated with conventional interfacial polymerization manufacturing. Additionally, the team uses the new process to incorporate fixed ionic groups into polyamide membranes to precisely engineer their properties via control of fixed ionic group concentration and cross-link density. Furthermore, the research team demonstrates that the electrospray additive manufacturing process can be used to manufacture membranes on a range of different substrates and that a resistances-in-series model can be used to inform the selection of support substrates.

This project explored a new way to manufacture advanced membranes, which are thin films that act as selective barriers to separate molecules, using a technique called molecular additive manufacturing. Membranes are critical for technologies that provide clean water and enable energy-efficient processes. Traditional membrane manufacturing methods, however, are limited to certain types of materials they can produce, and they often require the use of large amounts of solvent. This solvnt use makes these methods costly and environmentally taxing.

This project engineered an electrospray-based molecular additive manufacturing process to create polyamide membranes with precision structure. These membranes incorporate chemistry that allows them to conduct ions selectively. By controlling the ratios of the chemical building blocks used during printing, the team found that membrane conductivity can be engineered to meet different application specifications. The team also investigated how the underlying membrane support structure influences the overall membrane performance. Additionally, the team synthesized new linear sulfonated polyamide materials. These materials exhibited higher water uptake than expected, and this feature could translate into improved ionic conductivity, which is important for processes including electrodialysis and flow batteries. 

This project advanced fundamental understanding of how manufacturing methods influence membrane structure and performance. Additive manufacturing can overcome kinetic and thermodynamic limitations inherent to traditional interfacial membrane synthesis and manufacturing. The ability to precisely control membrane composition opens the door to designing next-generation membranes for desalination, energy storage, and other electrochemical systems.

Membrane technology plays a vital role in addressing global challenges related to water scarcity and sustainable energy. The manufacturing process developed in this project may reduce solvent and raw material use. These features may make this approach a more environmentally friendly alternative compared to conventional methods. The project also trained graduate and undergraduate students in advanced research techniques. Students engaged in outreach activities aimed at exposing the community to STEM topics. Finally, collaboration between the University of Virginia and the University of Connecticut supported professional growth. The project’s outcomes have been shared through peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, and webinars to ensure that the broader scientific community benefits from this project.

abstractText:
This project conducts a case study of attempts to reform regulation of a United States profession in the late 1990s and early 2000s, culminating in reforms enacted in 2002.  Professionals can use their expert knowledge in ways that cause harm to clients, third parties, and society in general.  A variety of regulatory approaches are possible for limiting or preventing such harm, including self-regulation, state regulation, or “regulation” by private market mechanisms.  Professions have traditionally regulated themselves, but in recent years many countries have seen a gradual shift away from this model toward an increasing regulatory role for states.  We know relatively little about why change is occurring in this particular direction.  This study is a step toward increasing our understanding that additionally permits the development of theory explaining how and why similar shifts toward increased state regulation of professions have occurred in a number of settings and might occur in the future.  More generally, the study sheds light on the circumstances that facilitate or impede change in the regulation of professional services, and begins to identify the limits on the possibilities open to societies to curb the misuse of expert knowledge.

The research design is a case study in which the interactions among key actors and stakeholder groups involved in seeking, resisting, and shaping state-based regulation during the late 1990s and the early 2000s are traced.  The case presents a kind of natural experiment: revelation of serious misconduct in the profession in 2001-2002 allows comparison of the same actors, decision options, and arguments before and after this key event.  The data are primarily documentary: speeches, transcripts of hearings, government reports, and articles from both the professional trade press and the general news media.  In addition to developing new theory and informing future efforts at regulatory change, the project will build intellectual bridges between the study of professions and other subfields and disciplines.  It will also contribute to revitalizing research on professional and expert work.

projectOutComesReport:
In recent years many countries have seen a shift away from self-regulation by professions toward increasing state involvement in professional regulation.  Existing explanations of professional regulatory arrangements explain them as resulting from a ?regulatory bargain? between the profession and the state, in which in which the state grants a professional community freedom from external regulation in return for the profession?s commitment to protect clients and the public from harm.  However, such theories do not help us to understand recent developments in which the state takes over regulatory authority despite the profession?s opposition.  This project sought to develop theory explaining this phenomenon by conducting a case study of two episodes involving efforts to reform the regulation of the accounting profession in the United States from 1996 to 2000 and from late 2001 to 2002.  The first episode was only modestly successful, resulting in fairly mild agency regulations, while the second episode led to the enactment of significant legislation. 

 

Through an analysis of Congressional and regulatory agency documents, speeches, newspaper and magazine articles, and interview transcripts, the study found that the same two processes operated during both episodes.  First, existing self-regulatory arrangements gradually became de-legitimated and de-institutionalized, due in part to the accounting profession?s own inattention to self-regulation while they pursued a new, more exciting and more lucrative vision of the profession.  Second, a different regulatory model ? involving a quasi-governmental body composed primarily of independent, public members ? gradually became legitimated and institutionalized.  During the first episode, these processes did not yet come to fruition.  A steady drip of accounting scandals, together with professional overreach in other areas, weakened the legitimacy of professional self-regulation but did not fully undermine it.  Meanwhile, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt acted as an institutional entrepreneur by proposing and promoting discussion of an independent quasi-governmental regulatory body.  The idea gained currency but did not become fully legitimated before the Clinton administration ended and Levitt left office.  These de-institutionalization and re-institutionalization processes were fully accomplished during the second episode, the bankruptcies of the Enron and WorldCom corporations helped to complete the de-legitimation of the existing self-regulatory system.  This process was also aided by the increasing distrust of rank-and-file, non-elite accountants, who perceived the elite professional association and elite firms as pursuing interests that they did not share, and who resoundingly rejected the elite?s vision of a broader, globalized profession in a formal vote.  At the same time, the idea of an independent quasi-governmental body was resurrected and became accepted as the best way forward.    

 

The first episode provided an essential prelude to the second.  The scandals of 2001 and 2002 were understood against the backdrop of the partial de-legitimation that occurred during the first episode, whereas without it they might have been seen merely as unfortunate but unusual incidents.  That partial destabilization also accentuated the cleavage between the elite and non-elite segments of the accounting profession, weakening non-elite support for the elite in their battle with the state in the second episode.  Moreover, the partial institutionalization of the idea of a quasi-governmental body during the first episode that these ideas achieved during the first episode made it much easier for policymakers to retrieve and adopt them during the second episode.  The findings here suggest, then, that successful shifts from professional self-regulation to quasi-governmental regulation are more likely to occur when a gradual de-institutionalization of self-regulatory arrangements has been going on for some time and an institutional entrepreneur makes some headway toward establishing acceptance of a new regulatory form.

title: The Expanding Role of the State in Professional Regulation

abstractText:
The Novel 2019 Coronavirus (COVID-19) has already caused unprecedented global social, economic, and health impact. This project will develop synthetic global multi-scale social contact networks. The synthetic but realistic social contact networks can capture human interactions either at an individual or community level. The networks can be used in conjunction with agent-based models to simulate the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. The simulations can in-turn be used to design and assess various interventions that balance health benefits with social and economic costs. Data will be made available to the scientific community. The PIs will also work with other research groups and continue their partnership with other federal and state agencies to support their response efforts.  

Developing synthetic social contact networks is a statistically and algorithmically challenging problem. This project will synthesize ensembles of two classes of synthetic social contact networks -- patch-based meta-population networks and individualized synthetic social contact populations and networks using a combination of machine learning and data driven modeling techniques. The need for such data driven mechanistic modeling methods has become abundantly clear in regimes when the available data is sparse and noisy. The project will undertake a detailed statistical analysis of the algorithms and the synthetic networks they produce. This includes methods to conduct global sensitivity analysis and methods to quantify the uncertainty in the outcomes as a function of the network structure. One of the many uses of this resource, is to support individual-based as well as meta-population-based simulation models for epidemic spread in general, and COVID-19 in particular.  Beyond supporting ongoing COVID-19 outbreaks, these synthetic social contact networks will be useful in responding to other epidemics. The PIs plan to make this data available to the global research community so that researchers around the world can immediately use it to assess the pandemic and the response efforts in their respective regions.

projectOutComesReport:
The work executed under this grant was motivated by the need to produce high quality openly available synthetic data sets for epidemic modeling, in particular for COVID-19. In light of this, care has been taken to base our work on data sets that are not commercial and that have few restrictions in their terms of use. The size and scope of the data generated under this grant is unique and we anticipate that the products will be broadly useful. The project was divided into three tasks.

The goal of Task 1 was to build synthetic networks compatible with a metapopulation representation of the region. Populations are grouped into sub-regions (aka patches) and the mobility or connectivity between the patches are generated through different modeling approaches. In addition to capturing the spatial heterogeneity in the population, such approaches can also be used to capture the age-stratification in contacts between the regions. We tackled this by constructing them at the administrative levels of 1 and 2 (state and county equivalent for the US), and using generative models or learned distributions for introducing connectivity.

The goal of Task 2 was to develop models and computational tools to construct synthetic populations for any country or region, often with only limited data available. The data products generated by the computational pipeline of models is being shared with the scientific community through Zenodo. Major accomplishments for this task are mainly the modeling, design, and implementation of an end-to-end chain of models alongside implementations of each model and their integration into a computational workflow. The construction is done at the spatial resolution of administrative level 2 (equivalent to a county for the US), and includes the following data for each region and the accompanying implementations used for their construction: base population, household grouping, activity sequences, activity locations and residence locations, activity location assignment, network construction, computational pipeline, validation and calibration, data collection efforts.

The goal of Task 3 was to create case studies to demonstrate the effective use of the populations and datasets developed in the first two tasks. A significant study involved vaccine allocation presented to the State Technical Advisory Committee, Karnataka, India (https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.05.26.21257836v1.full). 

The models, methods and data from our work can help advance computational epidemiology, which was one of the main motivators for the work. However, the population data generated in this work has a range of other application uses, a prominent example being analysis of socio-technical systems, that is, co-evolving and coupled systems composed of a human model (possibly including behavioral aspects) and collections of models of infrastructures such as transportation, power, communication, and the food supply chain. A prime example of such applications is evacuation scenarios tied to natural and human-initiated disasters, as well as most research addressed in NSF?s CRISP initiatives.
